lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The adverbial clause: definition, subordinators, the eight kinds, punctuation and a keyed exercise
objectives: Define an adverbial clause as a subordinate clause performing the adverbial function, and identify it by the subject-and-finite-verb test inside the group of words.

Name the usual subordinators of each kind - time, place, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result and manner - and classify a clause by the relation it expresses rather than by the isolated word.
Tell an adverbial clause from an adverbial phrase, and tell both from a noun clause, using the question the group answers and the structure inside it.
Punctuate an adverbial clause correctly when it is fronted and when it follows the main clause, and avoid the fragment and the comma splice.
Apply the time rule that a present or perfect form follows a time subordinator, and the unless rule that unless is not used for a contrary-to-fact condition.
Identify, classify, combine and correct adverbial clauses in a keyed, marked exercise.
lessons.body:
An adverbial is a part of a sentence, not a class of word. It is the element that answers a circumstantial question about the clause - when, where, why, how, how often, for how long, on what condition, with what result or despite what. The same job can be done in three different forms: by a single adverb (immediately), by an adverbial phrase (early in the morning) or by an adverbial clause (as soon as the bell rang). An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that performs the adverbial function of the clause it belongs to. Two tests fix the name. First, look inside the group of words: if it carries its own subject together with a verb that shows tense, it is a clause, so in as soon as the bell rang the bell is the subject and rang is a finite verb. Second, look at the whole group: if it can be moved to the front of the sentence or removed without wrecking the rest, it is an adverbial. The pupils stopped as soon as the bell rang becomes As soon as the bell rang, the pupils stopped, and either version still has a complete main clause. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a sentence; written by itself it is a fragment, not a sentence.
The word that introduces the clause is a subordinating conjunction, and it is the first signal of the kind: because marks a reason, although marks a concession, if marks a condition, when marks time, so that marks a purpose. Classify from the relation between the two clauses, never from the isolated word, because several words serve more than one kind and more than one class. Since introduces a reason in Since the road was flooded, we stayed indoors but marks time in She has lived in Ibadan since 2019; as introduces reason, time or manner; that is part of the subordinators so that and provided that but is a relative pronoun after a noun in the book that she borrowed. Ask what question the clause answers and paraphrase the relation, and the kind follows.
Because adverbial names a function while clause names a form, an adverbial clause must be told apart from an adverbial phrase, and the way to do it is to look inside the group rather than at what it tells you. Compare The dancers moved in time with the drum, where in time with the drum has no subject and no finite verb and is therefore a phrase, with The dancers moved as the drum beat, where the drum is a subject and beat is a finite verb, so the group is a clause. The same word can sit in either structure: after dinner is a prepositional phrase, while after we had dined is an adverbial clause, and after is a preposition in the first and a subordinating conjunction in the second. A quick substitution test confirms the answer: replace the group with a single adverb such as then, there or slowly. If one word can do the same job, the group is functioning as an adverbial; whether it is a phrase or a clause is decided by the subject-and-finite-verb test inside it. This lesson teaches the clause only. The scheme objective for Week 10 on adverbial and prepositional phrases is a separate objective and is not treated here, and nothing in this lesson is offered as coverage of it.
Punctuation follows position. When the adverbial clause comes first, a comma normally separates it from the main clause: If the bus is late, we will walk. When it comes after the main clause, the comma is normally unnecessary: We will walk if the bus is late. A clause of reason placed second is often still set off by a comma when the writer wants a pause before the explanation, and a purpose clause with so that usually is, but the rule a marker looks for is the fronted comma. Two errors follow from ignoring the structure. Two main clauses must never be joined by a comma alone: It was raining, we cancelled the trip is a comma splice; make one clause subordinate (Because it was raining, we cancelled the trip) or coordinate them (It was raining, so we cancelled the trip). And a subordinate clause must never be left standing as its own sentence: Because the generators failed twice. is a fragment; attach it to a main clause. Watch the difference between so and so that in those two corrected sentences: so joins two main clauses and is a coordinating conjunction, while so that introduces a subordinate purpose clause and is a subordinating conjunction.
Time and place. An adverbial clause of time answers when, how long or how often, and its common subordinators are when, while, as, before, after, since, until, once and as soon as: When the bell rang, the pupils carried their exercise books to the staff room. Time has one rule that examiners test again and again: after a time subordinator, English uses a present or a perfect form, not will - Write to me when you reach Kaduna, never When you will reach Kaduna. An adverbial clause of place answers where, and its subordinators are where and wherever: Where the path leaves the main road, a broken signpost still points to the health centre. Set the apparatus where every pupil in the back row can see it. Do not call every where-group an adverbial clause: in I know where she lives, the where-group is the object of knows and is a noun clause, while in Sit wherever you like it modifies sit and tells where, so it is an adverbial clause of place.
Reason and purpose. An adverbial clause of reason answers why, and is introduced by because, as, since, now that and seeing that: The practical was cancelled because the laboratory had no water. An adverbial clause of purpose answers why something was done with what end in view, and is introduced by so that, in order that and, in formal or older usage, lest: The teacher repeated the instruction twice so that no pupil would miss it. Keep the two apart by paraphrase. A reason clause explains why the main event happened - this happened, and this is the cause. A purpose clause names an aim the agent was trying to reach - this was done, and this is what it was meant to achieve. The test is whether the second clause could have failed: a purpose can fail (she studied hard but still lost the seat), a stated reason cannot, because if it did not cause the event it was not the reason. A purpose clause normally follows the main clause; bringing it first is formal: So that nobody would miss the instruction, the teacher repeated it twice.
Condition and concession. An adverbial clause of condition states the circumstance on which the main clause depends, with if, unless, provided that, providing that, as long as, so long as and on condition that: If the school bus starts by seven, the team will reach the venue before the practical begins. Unless means if ... not and is used for a real, present or future condition: You will not finish the paper unless you write faster. Do not use unless for a contrary-to-fact condition; if the council had repaired the bridge is not expressed as unless the council had repaired the bridge. An adverbial clause of concession states something that would be expected to prevent the main clause but does not, with although, though, even though, while in its contrast sense, whereas, no matter how and whatever: Although the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued. Condition and concession are distinguished by one question: does the main event happen only if the subordinate one does, or does it happen despite the subordinate one? The first is condition, the second is concession. Whereas and while in this sense contrast two facts, and the comma before the clause is normal when while opens the sentence: While the junior section used the hall, the senior section used the field.
Result and manner. An adverbial clause of result states what followed from a degree already expressed, and is built with so + adjective or adverb + that, and such a (or such + adjective + plural noun) + that: The queue was so long that the bell rang before Tunde reached the desk, and It was such a loud alarm that the whole block emptied in two minutes. The pair is one structure, so in an answer isolate the that-clause but credit the so ... that frame, and never treat so alone as the subordinator here. Result differs from purpose in direction: purpose names what the agent intended before the act, result names what in fact came after it. An adverbial clause of manner answers how or in what way, with as, as if and as though, and informally with the way: The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her. She answered the last question as if she had prepared it beforehand. As if and as though introduce a comparison with an imagined or doubtful state, and a past or subjunctive form after them signals that the speaker does not present the comparison as a fact.
How to work on these in a test. First, find the main clause - the part that could stand alone. Second, take the remaining group of words and apply the inside test: does it have its own subject and a verb showing tense? If yes it is a clause; if it has a preposition with a noun phrase, or only an adverb, it is a phrase and you are answering a different objective. Third, ask the circumstantial question the group answers and paraphrase the relation - when, where, why, on what condition, despite what, with what aim, with what result or in what way - then name the kind. Fourth, punctuate: put a comma after a fronted clause, take it away when the clause follows the main clause, and check that you have not left a fragment or written a comma splice. Worked example. In Although the market road was closed, the traders reached their stalls on foot, the main clause is the traders reached their stalls on foot; although the market road was closed has its own subject, the market road, and a finite verb, was closed, so it is a clause; it is not the condition for reaching the stalls but an obstacle they overcame, so it is concession; and it stands first, so the comma after it is required.

practice.question: Underline the adverbial clause in each sentence and state its kind (time, place, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result or manner). (1) Because the harmattan was severe, the form-two pupils watered the seedlings twice a day. (2) The electrician tested the socket after he had connected the earth wire. (3) Keep the samples where they will not be disturbed. (4) Although the market road was closed, the traders reached their stalls on foot. (5) She lowered her voice so that the class behind her could hear the answer. (6) The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her.
practice.answer: (1) Because the harmattan was severe - reason. (2) after he had connected the earth wire - time. (3) where they will not be disturbed - place. (4) Although the market road was closed - concession. (5) so that the class behind her could hear the answer - purpose. (6) as her instructor had shown her - manner.

marking.criterion: (1) clause located: Because the harmattan was severe
(2) clause located: after he had connected the earth wire
(3) clause located: where they will not be disturbed
(4) clause located: Although the market road was closed
(5) clause located: so that the class behind her could hear the answer
(6) clause located: as her instructor had shown her

practice.question: Say whether the words in capitals are an adverbial CLAUSE or an adverbial PHRASE, and give the structural reason for your answer. (1) The assembly ended BEFORE THE BELL. (2) The assembly ended BEFORE THE BELL RANG. (3) The pupils worked IN SILENCE. (4) The pupils worked AS IF THEY WERE BEING WATCHED.
practice.answer: (1) Phrase - the group has no subject and no finite verb; before takes the noun phrase the bell. (2) Clause - it has the subject the bell and the finite verb rang. (3) Phrase - in silence is a preposition with a noun and contains no verb. (4) Clause - it has the subject they and the finite verb were.

marking.criterion: (1) reason: no subject and no finite verb
(2) reason: subject the bell with finite verb rang
(3) reason: preposition with a noun and no verb
(4) reason: subject they with finite verb were

practice.question: Join the two sentences in each pair into one sentence, using the subordinator given in brackets, and punctuate correctly. (1) The inter-house final will be played. The rain stops by noon. (if) (2) The store keeper recorded every item. The auditor could check it later. (so that) (3) The hall emptied in two minutes. It was a loud alarm. (such ... that)
practice.answer: (1) If the rain stops by noon, the inter-house final will be played. (The present form stops follows the time-and-condition subordinator; a comma marks the fronted clause; if the pair is reversed the comma is dropped: The inter-house final will be played if the rain stops by noon.) (2) The store keeper recorded every item so that the auditor could check it later. (No comma is needed before a second-position purpose clause; so that must appear whole.) (3) It was such a loud alarm that the hall emptied in two minutes. (such a + adjective + noun, then the that-clause of result.)

marking.criterion: (1) both ideas subordinated with if, no fragment
(1) comma after the fronted clause (or none, correctly, after reversal) and present form after if
(2) purpose joined with the whole subordinator so that
(3) result that-clause completes the sentence with no comma splice

practice.question: Correct each of the following, which is a fragment, a comma splice or a wrong verb form, and say what was wrong. (1) Because the generators failed twice. (2) It was raining, we cancelled the trip. (3) I will call you as soon as you will arrive.
practice.answer: (1) Fragment: the because-clause has no main clause. Attach one - Because the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued. (2) Comma splice: two main clauses are joined by a comma alone. Subordinate one - Because it was raining, we cancelled the trip - or coordinate them - It was raining, so we cancelled the trip. (3) Wrong form after a time subordinator: will is not used in the as soon as clause. Correct - I will call you as soon as you arrive.

marking.criterion: (1) named as a fragment (no main clause)
(2) named as a comma splice (two main clauses, comma alone)
(3) corrected to a present form after as soon as
(3) reason given: a time subordinator takes a present or perfect form, not will

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The eight diphthongs: definition, spellings, accent variation and checked examples
objectives: Define a diphthong as one vowel sound that glides in quality within a single syllable, and tell it from a pure vowel and from the number of vowel letters in the spelling.
Name the eight diphthongs of the British teaching model in one consistent IPA set and state the accent the set belongs to.
Give two dictionary-checked example words for each diphthong with their usual spellings and some spelling variants, without treating spelling as a guide to sound.
Use pronunciation-dictionary entries to correct words placed under the wrong diphthong (brought, faults, Nassau, pear, poor, sure) and handle words with two accepted pronunciations (either, tour).
Describe the main differences between the UK and US dictionary entries for these sounds.
Complete a keyed, marked exercise, including two checked examples of each diphthong.
lessons.body:
A diphthong is a single vowel sound whose quality changes while it is being said: the tongue and lips start in one vowel position and glide towards another, all within one syllable. In day, the sound begins at a mid vowel and moves towards /ɪ/, yet you hear one vowel, not two. A pure vowel such as /iː/ in see keeps one steady quality from start to finish. Be careful with spelling: the spelling oy in boy represents a diphthong, while ea in beat represents a pure vowel. The test is always the sound a speaker produces, never the number of letters.
This lesson extends the earlier lesson on sound symbols and uses the same British reference model, shown in the UK entries of the Cambridge Dictionary. It does not claim that every accent of English has the same sounds. The eight diphthongs of this model are /eɪ/, /əʊ/, /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɔɪ/, /ɪə/, /eə/ and /ʊə/. If a list you have seen shows only seven, the missing one is /əʊ/. The first five end in a glide towards /ɪ/ or /ʊ/. The last three, /ɪə/, /eə/ and /ʊə/, end in a glide towards the central vowel /ə/. British dictionary entries may show an optional r after a vowel, as in here /hɪə(r)/; that /r/ is spoken only when a vowel follows. This lesson writes each diphthong without it.
Accents differ, and the dictionary shows it. The Cambridge US entries write /oʊ/ where the UK entries write /əʊ/ (go: UK /ɡəʊ/, US /ɡoʊ/). For the words here, care and tour, the US entries use a vowel followed by /r/ (here /hɪr/, care /ker/, tour /tʊr/) rather than the UK centring diphthongs. This is not a rule that every UK centring diphthong becomes a vowel plus /r/: idea has US /aɪˈdiː.ə/, with no /r/. Even inside the UK entries a word can have two forms, as tour does. So the eight-diphthong chart is a teaching convention for one model, not a fact about all English speech, and a learner should always say which model is being used.
/eɪ/ is the vowel of day /deɪ/ and plate /pleɪt/. It is spelled ay in day and a…e in plate (a, one consonant, then a silent e). It is also spelled ea in great, which the dictionary shows as /ɡreɪt/. Other spellings of /eɪ/ exist, but check any new word before using it as an example, because the same letters stand for different sounds in different words.
/əʊ/ is the vowel of go /ɡəʊ/ and boat /bəʊt/. It is spelled o in go, oa in boat and ow in grow /ɡrəʊ/. The US entries write it /oʊ/ (go /ɡoʊ/, boat /boʊt/); that is a difference of accent, not of word. Do not describe this sound as “the long o”: that names a letter, not a sound. Do not confuse /əʊ/ with /aʊ/: grow and now both end in ow, but grow has /əʊ/ and now has /aʊ/.
/aɪ/ is the vowel of sky /skaɪ/ and height /haɪt/. It is spelled y in sky and eigh in height; the dictionary itself uses the word eye as its key word for this sound. Either has two accepted pronunciations: the UK entry lists /ˈaɪðə(r)/ and /ˈiːðə(r)/, and the US entry lists the two the other way round. It is therefore not a safe fixed example of /aɪ/; if you use it, say which pronunciation you mean.
/aʊ/ is the vowel of now /naʊ/ and about /əˈbaʊt/. It is spelled ow in now and ou in about. Spelling is not a safe guide: Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, looks as if it contains /aʊ/, but the dictionary shows /ˈnæsɔː/, which ends in /ɔː/.
/ɔɪ/ is the vowel of boy /bɔɪ/ and noise /nɔɪz/. It is spelled oy in boy and oi in noise. Write the first symbol as the open-o /ɔ/, not with a capital or Cyrillic look-alike.
/ɪə/ is the vowel of here /hɪə(r)/ and idea /aɪˈdɪə/. It is spelled ere in here and ea in idea. The US entries do not use a diphthong here: here is /hɪr/ and idea is /aɪˈdiːə/, with two syllables after /aɪ/. Pear is not an example of /ɪə/: its UK entry is /peə(r)/, which has the next diphthong.
/eə/ is the vowel of care /keə(r)/ and heir /eə(r)/. It is spelled are in care and eir in heir. Air /eə(r)/ and wear /weə(r)/ show two more spellings, air and ear, and pear /peə(r)/ has the same vowel and spelling pattern as wear. In the US entries these words use /e/ followed by /r/ (care /ker/, heir /er/).
/ʊə/ is the vowel of pure /pjʊə(r)/ and tour /tʊə(r)/. It is spelled ure in pure and our in tour. It is the least stable of the eight. The UK entry for tour lists /tɔː(r)/ as well as /tʊə(r)/, and the UK entries for poor and sure show /pɔː(r)/ and /ʃɔː(r)/, with /ɔː/ and not /ʊə/, so poor and sure are not examples of /ʊə/ in this model. The US entries use /ʊ/ followed by /r/ (pure /pjʊr/, tour /tʊr/, poor /pʊr/).
Some class lists put words under the wrong sound. Check these against the UK entries: brought is /brɔːt/, not /eɪ/; fault is /fɒlt/, so faults is not an /əʊ/ word; Nassau is /ˈnæsɔː/, not /aʊ/; pear is /peə(r)/, not /ɪə/. Four spelling labels also need correcting from the spelling alone: hoe and foe are spelled oe, grow and thrown are spelled ow, eye is spelled eye, and air, fair and hair are spelled air.
To check a word, find its UK entry, read the vowel symbol between the consonants and match it to the eight above; then look at the US entry to see whether the accent changes the vowel. When you are asked for two examples of a diphthong, give two words whose entries you have checked, not words that only look similar. This lesson teaches symbol recognition from written dictionary entries. It does not test or certify how you say the sounds: listening to an authorised model and the teacher’s oral observation remain separate.

practice.question: Write the symbol of the diphthong in each word, using the British model of this lesson: day, go, sky, about, boy, idea, heir, tour.
practice.answer: day /eɪ/; go /əʊ/; sky /aɪ/; about /aʊ/; boy /ɔɪ/; idea /ɪə/; heir /eə/; tour /ʊə/ in the teaching model; also accept /ɔː/ if the learner identifies the alternative UK pronunciation, noting that this alternative is a pure vowel rather than a diphthong.

practice.question: Define a diphthong in one sentence and give one reason why the number of vowel letters in a word cannot tell you whether it has one.
practice.answer: A diphthong is one vowel sound that glides from one quality to another within a single syllable. The number of letters cannot decide it because spelling does not match sound: oy in boy represents a diphthong, whereas ea in beat represents a pure vowel.

marking.criterion: one vowel sound that changes quality (glides)
a reason or a contrasting pair showing that letters do not decide the sound

practice.question: Write the letters that spell the diphthong in each word: height, heir, idea.
practice.answer: height: eigh; heir: eir; idea: ea.

practice.question: A class list shows brought under /eɪ/, pear under /ɪə/ and Nassau under /aʊ/. For each word, say which vowel the Cambridge UK entry shows.
practice.answer: brought: /ɔː/, so it is not an /eɪ/ word. pear: /eə/, so it is not an /ɪə/ word. Nassau: /ɔː/ in its last syllable, so it is not an /aʊ/ word.

practice.question: Write two examples of each of the eight diphthongs: /eɪ/, /əʊ/, /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɔɪ/, /ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/. Use words whose Cambridge UK entries you have checked.
practice.answer: Model answer: /eɪ/ day, plate; /əʊ/ go, boat; /aɪ/ sky, height; /aʊ/ now, about; /ɔɪ/ boy, noise; /ɪə/ here, idea; /eə/ care, heir; /ʊə/ pure, tour. Accept any other word whose UK entry shows the target diphthong, for example great /ɡreɪt/ under /eɪ/, or air /eə(r)/ and wear /weə(r)/ under /eə/. Do not accept poor, sure, brought, faults, Nassau or pear under the diphthongs this lesson rejects them for; a word repeated within the same diphthong counts once; a US-only form does not count for /ɪə/, /eə/ or /ʊə/.

practice.question: (a) Write the Cambridge US transcription of go and of care. (b) Does every word with a UK centring diphthong acquire /r/ in the US entry? Use idea as evidence.
practice.answer: (a) go /ɡoʊ/; care /ker/. (b) No. Cambridge gives US idea as /aɪˈdiː.ə/, with no /r/.

marking.criterion: No, supported by the US transcription of idea without /r/.

lessons.title: Revision: matching the single vowel sounds /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/
objectives: Match words by vowel sound from the bracketed letters, not by spelling.
Identify the vowels /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/ and give key words for each.
Recognise the common spellings of each sound and the traps where the same letters stand for different sounds.
Distinguish the confusable pairs /ɪ/ and /iː/, /æ/ and /e/, /ʌ/ and /ʊ/, /ʌ/ and /ɑː/, /ɔː/ and /ɒ/, and /ɔː/ and /ɜː/.
State the accent model, and accept a stated variant such as the sounded r or the vowel of bath.
Answer a keyed, marked revision set and explain each key by the sounds of the options.
lessons.body:
This is a revision set on one skill: matching words by vowel sound when the target letters are shown in square brackets. It is built from the five Week 6 revision questions, which ask for the word with the same vowel sound as the letters underlined in the stem. The five stems test five different single vowel sounds, /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/, so they belong to the single-vowel teaching of Week 3 and not to the diphthongs that Week 6 teaches; this lesson is therefore labelled as revision and does not claim to assess the Week 6 scheme objectives. The source gives no key, its underlining appears only in the stems and is lost in the extracted text, and its options carry no marking of which letters count, so no answer is inferred from the options. Every word, item and answer below is newly written, and the square brackets do the work that the underline did in the source.
In a matching question the sound is the unit, not the spelling. First say the bracketed letters inside the whole word and listen for the vowel; then write its symbol; then test every option in the same way. Two words match when their stressed vowels are the same phoneme, even if the spellings are completely different. Two words with the same letters do not match if their vowels differ. The brackets may include letters that are not vowel letters: in north the bracketed letters are or, yet in the British model only the vowel /ɔː/ is heard, because an r before a consonant is not pronounced. Always match the vowel sound, not the number or the kind of letters.
The five sounds, each with key words, are these. /æ/ is the short vowel of cat, hand, lamp and glad, made with the jaw open. /ɪ/ is the short vowel of sit, gift and six, made with relaxed lips. /iː/ is the long vowel of see, team and key, made with spread lips. /ʌ/ is the short vowel of cup, sun and love, made with the mouth relaxed and open. /ɔː/ is the long vowel of saw, tall, corn and north, made with rounded lips. The length mark is part of the symbol: /iː/ and /ɔː/ are long, while /æ/, /ɪ/ and /ʌ/ are short. All five are monophthongs, so the vowel is held steady and does not glide as the diphthongs of the Week 6 teaching do.
Each sound has several common spellings. /æ/ is almost always written a, as in clap and sad. /ɪ/ is written i in sit and six, but also y in gym, u in busy, o in women and ui in build. /iː/ is written ee in see, ea in team, ey in key, ie in field, ei in seize and e in these. /ʌ/ is written u in cup and sun, o in come, son and love, ou in couple and young, and oo in blood. /ɔː/ is written or in fork and corn, aw in saw, a before ll in ball and wall, augh in caught, ough in thought, oor in door, and ar after w in warm. A learner who knows only the first spelling of each sound will miss many correct answers.
The same letters can stand for different vowels, which is why spelling cannot be used to choose an answer. The letters ea are /iː/ in team, /e/ in head and /eɪ/ in great. The letter u is /ʌ/ in cup, /ʊ/ in put and /ɪ/ in busy. The letter o is /ʌ/ in love, /uː/ in move, /əʊ/ in home and /ʊ/ in woman, but /ɪ/ in women. The letters oo are /ʌ/ in blood, /uː/ in food and /ʊ/ in book. In a well-made matching item the wrong options often look like the stem or like the right answer, so a word that looks right is exactly the word to check by sound.
Six contrasts cause most errors. /ɪ/ and /iː/ differ in length and quality: sit and seat are different words. /æ/ and /e/ differ in the height of the tongue and the opening of the jaw: bad and bed. /ʌ/ and /ʊ/ are both short and are often both written u: cut has /ʌ/ and put has /ʊ/, with rounder lips. /ʌ/ and /ɑː/ differ in length and position: cut and cart. /ɔː/ and /ɒ/ differ in length and rounding: caught and cot. /ɔː/ and /ɜː/ are both long vowels that are often written with or: north has /ɔː/, but worth has /ɜː/. When two options seem to match, test these contrasts first.
This lesson uses one model: British English as shown by a British pronunciation dictionary, with the symbol set of the earlier lessons. Accent matters in some words. In British English an r written after a vowel and before a consonant, or at the end of a word, is not pronounced, so north is /nɔːθ/ and car is /kɑː/; in American English the r is sounded, as in /nɔːrθ/ and /kɑːr/, and the vowel being matched is the same one with an r added. A few words change their vowel instead: bath has /ɑː/ in British English and /æ/ in American English, and top has /ɒ/ in British English and often /ɑː/ in American English. A fair item therefore uses words whose vowel is the same in both models, or states its accent in the key. The matching items in Q1 to Q3 use such words; Q6 uses bath on purpose, to practise stating an accent. A stated accent variant is correct when the key accepts it.
Use a fixed method for a matching item. First, read the stem and say the bracketed letters inside the word. Second, write the vowel symbol beside the stem. Third, say each option with its own bracketed letters and write its symbol. Fourth, choose the option whose symbol is identical, including the length mark. Fifth, if two options seem to match, check length first (/ɪ/ against /iː/), then the lips (/ʌ/ against /ʊ/ and /ɔː/), then accent. Sixth, do not choose an option because it contains the same letters or because it rhymes with the stem. A good key shows the stem symbol and each option’s symbol, as the keys below do, so that a wrong choice can be traced to the sound that was misheard.
Written matching shows that a learner can name sounds and ignore spelling. It does not by itself prove that the mouth makes the contrast reliably, and no written key can certify listening or speaking; pronunciation is assessed by oral observation with an authorised model, which is outside this written lesson. The practice below has six exercises of ten marks each, sixty marks in all: matching with four options A to D and exactly one correct option, naming the vowel, finding the odd one out, giving examples, correcting false rules and stating accent. Every item is original. The five parts of Q1 test the five sounds once each, and Q2 to Q5 revisit them from different directions.

practice.question: Choose the word, A to D, that has the same vowel sound as the letters in square brackets, and write the vowel symbol. (a) gl[a]d: A. p[a]ge B. l[a]mp C. c[a]r D. t[a]ll. (b) b[u]sy: A. b[u]s B. b[u]sh C. s[i]t D. s[ee]d. (c) k[ey]: A. gr[ey] B. h[ea]d C. t[ea]m D. s[i]x. (d) c[o]me: A. h[o]me B. l[o]ve C. m[o]ve D. w[o]man. (e) n[or]th: A. w[or]se B. c[or]n C. t[o]p D. f[ir]st.
practice.answer: (a) B, /æ/: glad and lamp both have /æ/; page is /eɪ/, car is /ɑː/ and tall is /ɔː/. (b) C, /ɪ/: the u in busy is /ɪ/ and sit has /ɪ/; bus is /ʌ/, bush is /ʊ/ and seed is /iː/. (c) C, /iː/: key and team both have /iː/; grey is /eɪ/, head is /e/ and six is /ɪ/. (d) B, /ʌ/: come and love both have /ʌ/; home is /əʊ/, move is /uː/ and woman is /ʊ/. (e) B, /ɔː/: north and corn both have /ɔː/ (an r is sounded after the vowel in American English); worse and first are /ɜː/, and top is /ɒ/ in British English. One mark for the option and one for the symbol in each part.

practice.question: Write the symbol of the vowel sound in the bracketed letters of each word, choosing from /æ ɪ iː ʌ ɔː/. (a) cl[a]p (b) w[o]men (c) f[ie]ld (d) bl[oo]d (e) w[a]ll.
practice.answer: (a) /æ/. (b) /ɪ/: the o in women is /ɪ/. (c) /iː/: ie is /iː/ in field. (d) /ʌ/: oo is /ʌ/ in blood, unlike food. (e) /ɔː/: a before ll is /ɔː/ in wall. The length mark must be written for /iː/ and /ɔː/; a symbol without it earns no mark.

practice.question: In each set, one word has a different vowel sound in the bracketed letters. Write the odd word and the symbol of the vowel shared by the other three. (a) s[ea]t, k[ey], h[ea]d, f[ie]ld. (b) l[o]ve, s[u]n, c[ou]ple, p[u]t. (c) c[a]t, h[a]nd, p[a]ge, s[a]d. (d) f[or]k, s[aw], b[a]ll, w[or]se. (e) s[i]t, b[u]sy, g[i]ft, p[ee]l.
practice.answer: (a) head: the others share /iː/; head has /e/. (b) put: the others share /ʌ/; put has /ʊ/. (c) page: the others share /æ/; page has /eɪ/. (d) worse: the others share /ɔː/; worse has /ɜː/. (e) peel: the others share /ɪ/; peel has /iː/. One mark for the odd word and one for the shared symbol in each set.

practice.question: Give two different words for each of the five sounds /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/. Do not use a word that appears in Q1 to Q3. Show the target letters in square brackets.
practice.answer: One model set, with other correct words accepted: /æ/ b[a]g, m[a]n; /ɪ/ p[i]n, b[i]g; /iː/ s[ee], m[ea]l; /ʌ/ c[u]p, s[o]n; /ɔː/ d[oo]r, p[or]t. Award one mark for each word whose stressed vowel is the named sound in the British model, with the target letters bracketed. Accept a word whose only difference from the British vowel is a sounded r in American English, as in door and port. Do not accept a word that shares only the spelling, such as head for /iː/, and do not accept the same word twice or a word with an accent-dependent vowel, such as bath for /æ/, unless the accent is stated.

practice.question: Each statement is false. Correct it and give one word as evidence. (a) The letters ea always stand for /iː/. (b) The letter u is always /ʌ/. (c) The sound /ɔː/ is always spelt or. (d) Sit and seat have the same vowel because the second differs only in spelling. (e) Words that end in the same letters always rhyme.
practice.answer: (a) ea can also be /e/ or /eɪ/: head has /e/ and great has /eɪ/. (b) u can be /ʊ/ or /ɪ/ as well: put has /ʊ/ and busy has /ɪ/. (c) /ɔː/ is also written aw, a before ll, augh and ough: saw and wall. (d) The vowels differ in length and quality: sit has /ɪ/ and seat has /iː/. (e) Spelling does not decide rhyme: love and move end in the same letters, but love has /ʌ/ and move has /uː/. One mark for the correction and one for the evidence in each part; any correct word of the same kind earns the evidence mark.

practice.question: For each word, write the British vowel symbol and say whether the American vowel differs. (a) b[a]th (b) n[or]th (c) c[a]r (d) gl[a]d (e) c[o]me.
practice.answer: (a) British /ɑː/; American /æ/, so the vowel differs; either vowel is acceptable only if the accent is named. (b) British /ɔː/; American has the same vowel with the r sounded, /ɔːr/, so the vowel quality is the same. (c) British /ɑː/; American has the same vowel with the r sounded, /ɑːr/, so the vowel quality is the same. (d) /æ/ in both. (e) /ʌ/ in both. One mark for the British symbol and one for the correct comparison in each part.

marking.criterion: (b) /ɔː/ and same vowel with sounded r
(c) /ɑː/ and same vowel with sounded r

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Vocabulary development: stock exchange and insurance
objectives: Define and use the eight stock-exchange terms in the Week 5 source glossary: stockbroker, security, stock, stock exchange, bond, shares, share certificate and debenture.
Distinguish equity (ownership) from debt (borrowing), and distinguish a stockbroker from a stock exchange.
Explain how a bond and a debenture represent debt, while shares represent ownership, without treating their issue terms as identical.
Define and use the original insurance vocabulary: insurer, insured, policyholder, policy, premium, coverage, exclusion, claim, beneficiary and risk.
Distinguish the insurer, policyholder, insured and beneficiary, and explain why a claim is assessed under the policy rather than paid automatically.
Use the vocabulary accurately in context and complete a keyed exercise with a total of 20 marks.
lessons.body:
This is an original SS1 vocabulary lesson for Week 5. It teaches the stock-exchange terms already listed in the source glossary and adds basic insurance vocabulary because the Week 5 scheme names insurance but the source does not teach its words. The examples and practice questions below are newly written. The lesson explains financial language; it is not investment or insurance advice.

A. STOCK EXCHANGE VOCABULARY

A stock exchange is an organised market where approved securities can be listed and traded under exchange rules. A company or government may raise funds by issuing securities; investors may later buy or sell listed securities through registered market operators. The Nigerian Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) explains that shares represent ownership, while bonds represent borrowing. This difference is central: buying a share makes an investor a part-owner of a company; buying a bond makes the investor a creditor of its issuer.

The source glossary contains these words:

1. Stock broker (stockbroker). A licensed or registered market professional who buys and sells securities for clients through the authorised market arrangements. A broker acts for a client; the broker is not automatically the owner of the securities. Example: “The investor asked a registered stockbroker to place an order for the shares.”

2. Security. A financial instrument that can be issued or traded, such as a share or a bond. The plural is securities. Example: “The company’s shares and its bonds are both securities, but they give investors different rights.”

3. Stock. In the source’s stock-exchange context, stock means shares or ownership interest in a company. Example: “When Femi bought the company’s stock, he acquired an ownership interest rather than lending the company money.” In other financial contexts, the word stock can have other meanings; use the context.

4. Stock exchange. The organised market on which listed securities are traded. The exchange provides a regulated marketplace; it does not guarantee that an investor will make a profit. Example: “The company applied to have its shares listed on the stock exchange.”

5. Bond. A debt security issued by a government or company. The issuer borrows money and promises to repay the principal according to the issue terms; interest may also be paid at stated times. The repayment date is often called the maturity date. A bondholder is a creditor, not a part-owner merely because the bond is held. Example: “The state issued a bond to borrow for a public project and stated the interest and maturity terms.” The source spells the heading as “Exhange” and one glossary entry as “securies”; the standard spellings are “exchange” and “securities”. The source also gives two different glosses for bond; this lesson uses one consistent meaning and does not treat the two entries as separate kinds of bond. These are learning corrections only: the original source text is not edited.

6. Shares. Units of ownership in a company. A shareholder owns a proportionate interest represented by the shares held and may have rights such as voting, depending on the class and terms of the shares. A company may declare dividends, but a dividend is not guaranteed. Example: “A shareholder may vote at a meeting if the shares carry voting rights.”

7. Share certificate. A document that records or evidences a person’s holding of specified shares. It may state the shareholder’s name and the number or class of shares. Shareholding records can also be maintained electronically, so a paper certificate should not be assumed to be the only record. Example: “The registrar checked the company’s records when the shareholder asked about a missing share certificate.”

8. Debenture. A debt instrument issued by a company. It records borrowing and the issuer’s repayment obligations; its interest, maturity and any security depend on the terms of issue. A debenture does not by itself make its holder a shareholder. Example: “The company raised borrowed funds by issuing a debenture, so the holder was a creditor under its terms.”

Do not confuse the main pairs. Shares or stock represent ownership; a bond or debenture represents debt. A stockbroker carries out a client’s securities transaction; the stock exchange provides the market where trading takes place. A security is the broad term that can include both shares and bonds. The source repeats bond with two different descriptions; for accurate use, learn the single debt-security meaning above and read the terms of a particular issue where detail matters.

B. INSURANCE VOCABULARY

Insurance is a contract that provides specified financial protection or a benefit when an event covered by the contract occurs. The customer pays a premium, and the insurer provides the cover described in the policy. The policy sets out what is covered, the limits and the conditions. Not every loss is covered.

1. Insurer. The insurance company that provides the cover under the policy. Example: “The insurer explained the documents needed before it could assess the claim.”

2. Insured. The person, property or interest protected by the policy. Example: “The insured vehicle was named in the motor policy.”

3. Policyholder. The person or organisation that owns or holds the insurance policy and is responsible for the policy obligations, including paying premiums where required. The policyholder and the insured may be the same person, but they are not always the same. Example: “A parent may be the policyholder on a policy that covers a child.”

4. Policy. The insurance contract and its written terms. It states the cover, limits, exclusions, premium and conditions. Example: “Before renewing the policy, the policyholder read the section explaining what the cover excluded.”

5. Premium. The amount paid to the insurer for the insurance cover. It may be paid at agreed intervals or as a single payment, depending on the policy. Example: “The policyholder paid the annual premium to keep the cover in force.”

6. Coverage (cover). The protection provided by the policy: the events, losses or benefits included, subject to limits and conditions. Example: “The policy provided coverage for specified fire damage, up to the stated limit.”

7. Exclusion. A risk, event or circumstance that the policy says it does not cover. Example: “The policy’s exclusion section explained that the particular loss was not covered.”

8. Claim. A formal request to the insurer for payment or a benefit after an event that may be covered. The insurer assesses the claim against the policy; making a claim does not automatically mean it will be paid. Example: “After the accident, the policyholder submitted a claim with the documents requested by the insurer.”

9. Beneficiary. A person named to receive a policy benefit, commonly under a life policy. The beneficiary may be different from the policyholder or the insured. Example: “The policy named Aisha as the beneficiary who would receive the stated life-policy benefit if the policy conditions were met.”

10. Risk. The possibility of a loss or harmful event that may be covered by insurance. Example: “The insurer considered the risk described in the application before deciding the terms of cover.”

C. USING THE WORDS ACCURATELY

Read the surrounding sentence before choosing a meaning. In a stock-exchange passage, stock usually refers to company shares; in a shop, stock may mean goods kept for sale. A bond is a debt instrument, not a share. A debenture is also a company debt instrument, but its exact rights and security depend on its issue terms. Do not say that every security gives ownership.

In insurance, distinguish the people and the documents. The insurer provides the cover; the policyholder holds the contract; the insured is the person or interest protected; the beneficiary receives a stated benefit where named. The premium is the payment for cover. A claim is the request made after a possible insured event. Coverage and exclusions must be read together: a policy may cover one type of loss and exclude another. The policy wording and applicable law determine the actual result.

A useful memory check is to ask four questions: Is the word about ownership or borrowing? Is it a person, a document or a payment? Does it describe what is covered or what is excluded? Is it a request for a benefit or the benefit itself? These questions help you choose a meaning that fits the context.

practice.question: Match each term to the correct meaning. Write the letter of the meaning beside each term. Terms: (a) stockbroker (b) security (c) bond (d) shares (e) stock exchange (f) debenture (g) premium (h) claim. Meanings: (1) a formal request for an insurance payment or benefit; (2) units of ownership in a company; (3) a registered professional who trades securities for clients; (4) an amount paid for insurance cover; (5) a debt instrument issued by a government or company; (6) an organised market for listed securities; (7) a broad term for a financial instrument such as a share or bond; (8) a company-issued debt instrument.

For each statement, write EQUITY (ownership) or DEBT (borrowing). (a) An investor buys ordinary shares in a company. (b) A state government issues a bond and promises repayment under its terms. (c) A company raises borrowed funds by issuing a debenture. (d) A person holds shares that carry voting rights in a company.
practice.answer: (a) EQUITY: shares represent ownership. (b) DEBT: the bond represents money borrowed by the issuer. (c) DEBT: a debenture is a company debt instrument. (d) EQUITY: shares represent ownership; voting rights depend on their class and terms.

practice.question: Complete each sentence with the correct word from this list: insurer, insured, premium, exclusion. Use each word once. (a) The company that provides the insurance cover is the ______. (b) The person or property protected by the policy is the ______. (c) The payment made for the cover is the ______. (d) A circumstance that the policy does not cover is an ______.
practice.answer: (a) insurer. (b) insured. (c) premium. (d) exclusion.

practice.question: Read the situation. Amina takes out a life-insurance policy on herself, pays the required amount to keep it active and names her brother Musa to receive the stated benefit if the insured event occurs and the policy conditions are met. (a) Who is the policyholder? (b) Who is the insured? (c) Who is the beneficiary? (d) What is the payment Amina makes called? (e) If Musa later asks the insurer to pay the benefit, what is the request called, and is payment automatic?
practice.answer: (a) Amina is the policyholder. (b) Amina is also the insured because the policy protects her life. (c) Musa is the beneficiary because he is named to receive the stated benefit. (d) The payment is the premium. (e) The request is a claim. Payment is not automatic: the insurer assesses it against the policy terms, exclusions and conditions.

marking.criterion: Identifies Amina as policyholder and insured (both roles)
Names the payment as the premium
Names the request as a claim and explains that it is assessed under the policy, not automatically paid

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Original comprehension practice: a community seed-saving group (Week 5 parallel assignment)
objectives: Read an original informational passage and locate explicit details.
Infer a reasonable conclusion from stated evidence.
Use context to interpret vocabulary.
Identify a suitable title and the main organising idea.
Answer a keyed ten-item multiple-choice comprehension exercise.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT ACTIVITY — Week 5 weekend assignment. The source refers to Countdown Passage C, questions 31–40, pages 354–355, but does not include the passage, questions, answers, author/edition evidence or a verified key. This passage and all ten questions are original; they are not represented as Countdown content.

**A Community Seed-Saving Group**

At the end of each harvest, a group of farmers in Oke-Ayo village selects healthy seeds from crops that have grown well in the local soil. The farmers formed the group because some useful varieties were becoming difficult to find in nearby markets. By saving seeds together, members can preserve varieties that suit their farms and share them with neighbours.

Before the next planting season, two members inspect the stored seeds. They remove damaged pieces, place each variety in a clean, dry container and attach a label showing its name and collection date. The containers are kept away from damp walls because moisture can cause seeds to spoil. The group also tests a small sample to find out whether the seeds are still viable—that is, able to germinate and grow.

Each member records the quantity received and agrees to return a fair quantity of healthy seeds after harvest. The arrangement does not guarantee a large crop: rainfall, soil conditions and careful farming still matter. However, the shared store gives members access to varieties they may not have saved themselves and helps the village keep a record of useful local crops.

**Answer questions 1–10. Choose the best answer.**

practice.question: According to the passage, What is the main reason the farmers formed the seed group? Choose the best answer: A. To save and share locally suitable seeds; B. To sell farm machines; C. To build a market; D. To stop all planting.
practice.answer: A. To save and share locally suitable seeds

practice.question: According to the passage, Which action takes place before the planting season? Choose the best answer: A. After harvest; B. Before the planting season; C. During a storm; D. Only at market.

objectives: Explain the two purposes of advertising: informing an audience and creating or stimulating demand through persuasion.
Locate explicit information and make evidence-based inferences in an original passage about advertising.
Interpret vocabulary in context and distinguish verifiable facts from promotional claims.
Answer marked comprehension questions using evidence from the passage.
Deliver a short, clear oral announcement and identify its informative and persuasive elements.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT ACTIVITY — Week 6 advertising comprehension and oral skills. The scheme refers to Effective English pages 86–87, but that passage and its questions are not included. This passage, questions and oral task are independently written; they are not a reproduction of the textbook.

**A Better Way to See at Night**

When the evening study period begins, some pupils in Akinyele village find it difficult to read during power cuts. A local cooperative has therefore arranged a demonstration of rechargeable solar study lamps at the community hall on Saturday. The lamps collect energy from sunlight during the day and can provide light for several hours after sunset. Visitors will be able to examine the lamps, ask about charging time and compare the available sizes.

The notice gives practical information: the place, date, time and features of the product. It also uses persuasive language, describing the lamps as a convenient option for families who need light during an interruption to electricity supply. Its purpose is not simply to announce that a lamp exists. It aims to encourage interested people to attend the demonstration and consider whether the product meets their needs.

A responsible reader should separate verifiable information from promotional claims. The date and venue can be checked with the cooperative. A statement about how long a lamp works should be tested or supported by clear product information. Advertising can inform an audience and can also stimulate demand by presenting a product attractively. Readers should compare claims, ask questions and make decisions without assuming that every advertisement is complete or unbiased.

**Comprehension questions**
1. What difficulty do some pupils experience?
2. What is being demonstrated, and where?
3. State two pieces of practical information in the notice.
4. How does the notice try to persuade readers?
5. Explain the meaning of *verifiable* in context.
6. Why should readers ask questions about product claims?
7. Identify the two purposes of advertising described in the passage.
8. Give one difference between informing an audience and stimulating demand.

**Oral task.** In pairs, deliver a 45–60 second spoken announcement for a useful school service (for example, a library reading hour). State the service, time/place and one benefit. Then identify which sentence informs listeners and which sentence attempts to persuade them. Speak clearly, use a suitable pace and do not make unsupported claims.

lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT ACTIVITY — Week 6 weekend assignment. The source names Countdown questions 41–60 on pages 355–357, but neither the questions nor their answers are present, and the source references give a different Countdown author. These are original integrated revision questions based on Week 6 topics in this package, not a claim about the missing book's contents or a reproduction of its questions.

Choose one answer (A–D) for each question. Each is worth one mark; total 20.

1. Which sentence informs a reader rather than persuading the reader?
A. The library opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays.
B. Buy this wonderful book today!
C. You must choose our service.
D. Our product is the best ever.

2. Which statement is a verifiable fact?
A. This is the most exciting event.
B. The meeting begins at 10 a.m. in Room 4.
C. Everyone will love the programme.
D. This is surely the finest school.

3. What is the main purpose of a simile?
A. To compare using like or as
B. To give a human action to an object
C. To ask for information
D. To repeat a sound

4. Which sentence contains personification?
A. The wind whispered through the trees.
B. The bag is heavy.
C. She ran quickly.
D. The room was large.

5. Which is a rhetorical question?
A. Where is the library?
B. Have you submitted the form?
C. Who would refuse a chance to learn?
D. When does the lesson begin?

6. Choose the correct diphthong description.
A. A glide between two vowel qualities within one syllable
B. Two separate syllables
C. Any two written vowel letters
D. A consonant followed by a vowel

7. Which word commonly contains the /eɪ/ sound in the British teaching model?
A. day
B. boy
C. now
D. near

8. Which sentence contains an adverbial clause of reason?
A. Because the road was flooded, the bus arrived late.
B. The bus is yellow.
C. The driver smiled.
D. The late bus stopped.

9. In 'Although the rain continued, the match began', the opening clause expresses:
A. time
B. concession
C. place
D. purpose

10. Which is the best topic sentence for a descriptive paragraph about a busy market?
A. The market was crowded with movement, colour and sound.
B. Markets are important.
C. I went there last year.
D. There are many shops.

11. Which detail appeals most directly to the sense of smell?
A. The sharp scent of ripe oranges filled the stall.
B. A blue umbrella stood nearby.
C. The bell rang loudly.
D. The floor felt rough.

12. Which order is most suitable for describing a room?
A. A clear spatial order, such as doorway to window
B. Random unrelated facts
C. Only the writer's travel history
D. A list of arguments

13. Which sentence is a complex sentence?
A. The bell rang.
B. The bell rang, and pupils stood.
C. When the bell rang, pupils stood.
D. Stand up!

14. Which word is a subordinating conjunction in 'We waited because the rain was heavy'?
A. waited
B. because
C. rain
D. heavy

15. Which linking expression signals a result?
A. however
B. for example
C. as a result
D. first

16. What should a conclusion in an expository essay do?
A. Introduce an unrelated topic
B. Briefly draw together the explanation
C. Add an unsupported claim
D. Repeat every sentence word for word

17. Which is the most objective expository sentence?
A. The process has three stages: sorting, washing and drying.
B. This is obviously the best process ever.
C. Nobody could disagree with me.
D. The process is amazing and perfect.

18. Which phrase best signals a contrast?
A. therefore
B. however
C. next
D. for instance

19. Which action best checks an advertisement's product claim?
A. Accept it because it is colourful
B. Compare it with reliable product information
C. Assume every claim is complete
D. Ignore the stated conditions

20. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
A. If the rain stops, the team will practise.
B. If the rain stops the team, will practise.
C. If, the rain stops the team will practise.
D. If the rain stops the team will, practise.

Answer key: 1 A; 2 B; 3 A; 4 A; 5 C; 6 A; 7 A; 8 A; 9 B; 10 A; 11 A; 12 A; 13 C; 14 B; 15 C; 16 B; 17 A; 18 B; 19 B; 20 A.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Transport vocabulary: aviation, maritime, rail and road
objectives: Use accurate aviation vocabulary in context, including inclusive names for flight crew and airport facilities.
Distinguish maritime vessels, parts, port facilities and shipbuilding/repair places, and use the terms in context.
Distinguish a locomotive, passenger coach or carriage, freight wagon, track, station, platform and railway signals.
Use road-transport vocabulary for vehicles, road spaces, junctions and pedestrian facilities.
Write ten coherent aviation sentences using the target vocabulary.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — Transport vocabulary in context

Transport is the movement of people or goods from one place to another. Means of transport may be grouped by the route they use: air, water, rail or road. Learn each word with the job or place it names, then use it in a sentence. The explanations and examples below are newly authored for this lesson, not a corrected transcription of the source lists.

AIR TRANSPORT
An aircraft is a machine designed for flight. A pilot operates it; a co-pilot assists the pilot. Cabin crew members look after passengers and cabin safety. “Cabin crew” or “flight attendant” names the role without assuming the worker's age or gender. An airport is the place where aircraft and passengers are handled. A runway is the prepared strip on which aircraft take off and land. A taxiway is the route aircraft use to move between a runway and other airport areas. A hangar is a large building where aircraft are kept or maintained. The control tower is the facility from which air traffic controllers coordinate aircraft movements. A boarding pass identifies a passenger's flight and boarding details; a boarding gate is where passengers enter the departure process. A terminal is the airport building used by passengers.

Ten aviation sentence models:
1. The pilot checked the flight instruments before departure.
2. The co-pilot confirmed the route with the pilot.
3. The aircraft moved slowly along the taxiway.
4. The air traffic controller cleared the aircraft to approach the runway.
5. The aircraft took off from the runway after the final checks.
6. Passengers showed their boarding passes at the gate.
7. The cabin crew welcomed passengers and explained the safety procedures.
8. The ground team loaded the checked baggage into the aircraft.
9. Engineers inspected the aircraft inside the hangar.
10. The terminal became busy when several flights arrived.

MARITIME TRANSPORT
A vessel is a ship or boat used on water. The bow is its front and the stern its rear. The hull is the main body of the vessel; the deck is the floor-like surface on which people may work or move. The bridge is the area from which a ship is navigated. When facing towards the bow, port is the vessel's left side and starboard its right side. A berth is a designated place where a vessel can be secured in a port; the word can also mean a sleeping place on a ship. A quay is a structure beside water where vessels can come alongside for people or cargo. “Dock” can refer to a sheltered area or facility where vessels are loaded, unloaded or serviced; its exact use depends on the facility. A shipyard is a place where ships are built or repaired. A boatyard usually serves smaller boats. Do not use “shipyard”, “boatyard”, “dock”, “quay” and “berth” as if they all named the same thing. A row is an action performed with oars; an oar is the implement used to propel a small boat. “International waters” is a legal expression, not a simple synonym for any sea or ocean; do not assign it an invented boundary in a vocabulary exercise.

RAIL TRANSPORT
A train is a connected set of railway vehicles that travels on rails. A locomotive is the engine that pulls or powers a train. A passenger coach or carriage carries passengers; a freight wagon carries goods. In this rail context, a coach is one vehicle in the train, not the whole train. The track is the railway route on which the train runs. A station is where passengers board and leave trains. A platform is the raised area beside the track where passengers wait and board. Railway signals communicate instructions to train operators, while points allow a train to be directed from one track to another. A level crossing is where a railway line crosses a road.

ROAD TRANSPORT
A road vehicle travels on a road; examples include a car, bus, lorry or motorcycle. The driver operates the vehicle and passengers travel in it. A road lane is a marked part of the carriageway for a line of traffic. A carriageway is the part of a road used by vehicles; on a divided road, each direction may have a separate carriageway. A pavement (British English) is the path beside a road for pedestrians; in some varieties of English, “sidewalk” is used. A verge is the strip of ground at the side of a road. A junction is a place where roads meet, and a roundabout is a circular junction around which traffic travels. A pedestrian crossing is a marked place for people to cross. A bus stop is a designated place where a bus picks up or sets down passengers. Use the regional term that suits the context, and distinguish the road itself from the vehicles travelling on it.

Use precise vocabulary: a locomotive is not the whole train; a runway is not a taxiway; a quay is not a shipyard; and a carriageway is not the pavement. A good sentence makes the relationship clear.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Noun clauses: the five functions and their correct analysis
objectives: Define a noun clause as a subordinate clause doing a noun-like function and identify its clause structure.
Identify noun clauses functioning as subject and direct object, building on the existing Week 7 mapping.
Analyse noun clauses functioning as subject complements after linking verbs.
Analyse noun clauses functioning as complements of prepositions and distinguish them from object complements.
Analyse noun clauses functioning as object complements and correct the source's swapped complement labels.
Write five sentences containing noun clauses and identify the function of each clause.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — The five noun-clause functions

A clause contains a verb and its subject (which may be understood from context). A noun clause is a subordinate clause that occupies a position commonly filled by a noun phrase. Its function is identified by the work it does in the larger sentence, not simply by the word that introduces it. The words what, whoever, whether and that can introduce noun clauses, but a word such as that does not make every following group a noun clause: check for a clause and its function.

The existing Week 7 lesson already defines clauses and identifies noun clauses as subject and object. Keep those mappings: in “What she wrote pleased us”, “What she wrote” is the subject; in “We know that she arrived”, “that she arrived” is the direct object of know. The examples below extend that teaching to the three complement functions and practise all five functions together.

1. SUBJECT
A noun clause can be the subject of the main clause. In “What she decided surprised the class”, the clause “What she decided” is the subject of surprised. Ask what surprised the class; the answer is the whole clause.

2. OBJECT OF A VERB
A noun clause can be the direct object of a verb. In “I remember what the teacher explained”, the clause “what the teacher explained” is the object of remember. The verb remember takes that clause as the thing remembered.

3. SUBJECT COMPLEMENT
A subject complement follows a linking verb and identifies or describes the subject. In “The question is what we should do next”, the clause “what we should do next” completes the meaning of the subject question after the linking verb is. It is a subject complement, not an object.

4. COMPLEMENT OF A PREPOSITION
A preposition can take a noun clause as its complement. In “The prize will go to whoever wins”, the clause “whoever wins” completes the preposition to. The whole prepositional phrase is “to whoever wins”. Another example is “We were surprised by what the guide explained”: the clause “what the guide explained” is the complement of by. This is the correct analysis of the source's example “The prize will go to whoever wins”; it is not an object complement.

5. OBJECT COMPLEMENT
An object complement follows and completes the meaning of a direct object, often by identifying or naming it. In “The committee named the proposal what the members suggested”, “the proposal” is the direct object of named and the clause “what the members suggested” identifies the name given to that object; it functions as object complement. The source's example “We call him what he likes” belongs to this object-complement pattern: “him” is the object and “what he likes” completes it. It is not a prepositional complement because no preposition introduces the clause.

How to analyse a sentence:
- Find the subordinate clause and mark its subject and verb.
- Identify the word or phrase that the clause belongs with in the main clause.
- Ask what role the whole clause plays: subject, object of a verb, subject complement, complement of a preposition or object complement.
- Do not confuse a clause's function with the function of the whole prepositional phrase around it. In “to whoever wins”, the clause is the complement of to; “to whoever wins” is the prepositional phrase.

The label “complement” describes a relationship in sentence structure. A subject complement relates to the subject through a linking verb; an object complement relates to the direct object; a prepositional complement completes a preposition. A phrase or clause should be classified by its actual position and relationship, not by a copied heading.

practice.question: In each sentence, identify the noun clause and state its function: (a) What she decided surprised the class. (b) I know that the bus has arrived. (c) The question is whether the route is safe. (d) The prize will go to whoever wins. (e) The committee named the proposal what the members suggested. (10 marks)
practice.answer: (a) “What she decided” — subject. (b) “that the bus has arrived” — direct object of know. (c) “whether the route is safe” — subject complement after is. (d) “whoever wins” — complement of the preposition to. (e) “what the members suggested” — object complement of the direct object the proposal.

marking.criterion: (a) correctly identifies the clause and subject function
(b) correctly identifies the clause and direct-object function
(c) correctly identifies the clause and subject-complement function
(d) correctly identifies the clause and prepositional-complement function
(e) correctly identifies the clause and object-complement function

practice.question: Correct the two source headings for these examples: (a) “We call him what he likes”; (b) “The prize will go to whoever wins”. (2 marks)
practice.answer: (a) “what he likes” is an object complement; (b) “whoever wins” is the complement of the preposition “to”. The source has these two labels swapped.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The 24 English consonant sounds: place, manner, voicing and examples
objectives: Identify the 24 consonant phonemes in one consistent British English teaching model.
Classify each consonant by place of articulation, manner of articulation and voicing.
Recognise two checked example words for each consonant phoneme.
Use IPA symbols accurately and distinguish English /r/ from the IPA alveolar trill, and /j/ from a voiceless sound.
Complete a keyed exercise giving two example words for each of ten specified consonants.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — The 24 consonant phonemes in a British English teaching model

A consonant is described by three main features:
• Place of articulation: where the airflow is narrowed or stopped in the vocal tract.
• Manner of articulation: how the airflow is stopped, narrowed or allowed to pass.
• Voicing: whether the vocal folds vibrate. Put two fingers lightly on the front of your throat: you can often feel vibration for a voiced sound and not for its voiceless partner. This is a simple demonstration, not a pronunciation assessment.

The table below uses one consistent British English teaching model with 24 consonant phonemes. The examples show the sound, not just the spelling. A phoneme may be written with one symbol (/p/) or two symbols (/tʃ/, /dʒ/); the latter are single affricate phonemes in this model. Accent variation exists, so do not assume every English speaker uses an identical inventory or pronunciation.

| IPA sound | Place | Manner | Voicing | Two example words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /p/ | bilabial (both lips) | plosive | voiceless | pen, cap |
| /b/ | bilabial | plosive | voiced | bad, rub |
| /t/ | alveolar (tongue at the ridge behind upper teeth) | plosive | voiceless | tea, set |
| /d/ | alveolar | plosive | voiced | day, red |
| /k/ | velar (back of tongue at soft palate) | plosive | voiceless | key, take |
| /ɡ/ | velar | plosive | voiced | get, rug |
| /f/ | labiodental (lower lip and upper teeth) | fricative | voiceless | fine, life |
| /v/ | labiodental | fricative | voiced | van, love |
| /θ/ | dental (tongue at or near teeth) | fricative | voiceless | thin, bath |
| /ð/ | dental | fricative | voiced | this, then |
| /s/ | alveolar | fricative | voiceless | soon, bus |
| /z/ | alveolar | fricative | voiced | zero, days |
| /ʃ/ | postalveolar (just behind the alveolar ridge) | fricative | voiceless | ship, wish |
| /ʒ/ | postalveolar | fricative | voiced | vision, pleasure |
| /h/ | glottal (at the vocal folds) | fricative | voiceless | hat, behind |
| /tʃ/ | postalveolar | affricate (stop followed by frication) | voiceless | chain, catch |
| /dʒ/ | postalveolar | affricate | voiced | jam, bridge |
| /m/ | bilabial | nasal | voiced | milk, come |
| /n/ | alveolar | nasal | voiced | nice, on |
| /ŋ/ | velar | nasal | voiced | sing, long |
| /l/ | alveolar | lateral approximant | voiced | light, hole |
| /r/ (often realised [ɹ]) | postalveolar | approximant | voiced | red, carry |
| /j/ | palatal (front of tongue near hard palate) | approximant | voiced | yes, young |
| /w/ | labio-velar (lips rounded, back of tongue raised) | approximant | voiced | wet, well |

MANNER GROUPS
1. Plosives /p b t d k ɡ/: the airflow is briefly stopped and then released.
2. Fricatives /f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h/: air passes through a narrow opening and creates friction.
3. Affricates /tʃ dʒ/: a stop release moves directly into frication; each is treated as one consonant phoneme here.
4. Nasals /m n ŋ/: the mouth is closed at the place of articulation and air passes through the nose.
5. Approximants /l r j w/: the articulators approach one another without the strong friction of a fricative. /l/ is lateral because air passes around the sides of the tongue.

VOICING PAIRS
The following pairs differ mainly in voicing: /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /k/–/ɡ/, /f/–/v/, /θ/–/ð/, /s/–/z/, /ʃ/–/ʒ/, and /tʃ/–/dʒ/. The first sound in each pair is voiceless; the second is voiced. The remaining consonants in this 24-sound model are voiced except /h/, which is voiceless.

IMPORTANT IPA AND SOURCE CORRECTIONS
The International Phonetic Association chart arranges consonants by place and manner; where a pair shares a cell, the symbol on the right is voiced and the one on the left is voiceless. Do not treat ordinary letter shapes as IPA symbols. The English /r/ phoneme is commonly written /r/ in broad learner transcriptions; its usual British sound is the postalveolar approximant [ɹ], not the IPA alveolar trill [r]. The /j/ in yes is a voiced palatal approximant, not a voiceless sound. The /t/ in tea is alveolar, not velar; /k/ is velar. The affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are single phonemes in this model, not two unrelated consonants.

The source's Week 7 table contains incorrect place/voicing labels and doubtful or non-IPA lookalikes in its examples. Those defects remain recorded against the original source; this newly authored table supplies a checked teaching reference rather than rewriting the source. The word examples are checked against established British pronunciation guides. This lesson assesses classification and example recognition only. It does not claim to assess a learner's spoken performance; oral pronunciation assessment and audio evidence remain deferred.

practice.question: Give two example words for each of these ten consonant sounds: /p/, /b/, /t/, /k/, /f/, /θ/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, /m/ and /ŋ/. Use words in which the target sound is clearly present. (20 marks)
practice.answer: /p/: pen, cap. /b/: bad, rub. /t/: tea, set. /k/: key, take. /f/: fine, life. /θ/: thin, bath. /ʃ/: ship, wish. /tʃ/: chain, catch. /m/: milk, come. /ŋ/: sing, long.

practice.question: Classify these four sounds by place, manner and voicing: /p/, /v/, /ŋ/ and /dʒ/. (12 marks)
practice.answer: /p/: bilabial, plosive, voiceless. /v/: labiodental, fricative, voiced. /ŋ/: velar, nasal, voiced. /dʒ/: postalveolar, affricate, voiced.

marking.criterion: /p/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/v/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/ŋ/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/dʒ/ has correct place, manner and voicing
