lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 8 original revision: word stress, contextual meaning and debate
objectives: Identify primary word stress in five multisyllabic words.
Choose context-appropriate synonyms for five vocabulary items.
Prepare a respectful debate speech supporting or opposing a motion.
lessons.body:
This is an original revision set for Week 8. It does not reproduce or supply answers to the unavailable textbook tasks. Use the pronunciation guidance taught in class: a word's primary stress is the syllable spoken most strongly. In the broad British pronunciations below, the mark ˈ comes immediately before the primary-stressed syllable. Say each word aloud and compare the stressed syllable; do not guess from spelling alone.
Word-stress review: indoctrinate /ɪnˈdɒktrɪneɪt/ (second syllable); refinery /rɪˈfaɪnəri/ (second); phenomenal /fəˈnɒmɪnəl/ (second); consistency /kənˈsɪstənsi/ (second); acrobatic /ˌækrəˈbætɪk/ (third; the earlier ˌ marks secondary stress).
Meaning in context: momentarily means for a very short time; stealthily means secretly or quietly to avoid being noticed; squarely can mean directly or firmly; meticulous means extremely careful and attentive to detail; satisfied means pleased because a need or expectation has been met. Choose a synonym that fits the sentence, not merely one that shares a general topic.
A debate speech addresses a motion and tries to persuade an audience. State whether you support or oppose the motion, define any important term, give two or three clear reasons with examples, respond respectfully to an opposing point, and finish with a memorable conclusion. For the motion “Participation of women in government should be encouraged”, either side may be argued. A respectful opposing argument must address policy or implementation, not attack people because of sex or identity.

practice.question: For each word, state the syllable carrying primary stress: (a) indoctrinate; (b) refinery; (c) phenomenal; (d) consistency; (e) acrobatic.
practice.answer: (a) second; (b) second; (c) second; (d) second; (e) third.

practice.question: Choose the closest meaning in each context: (a) The lights went out momentarily. (briefly / permanently) (b) The thief moved stealthily. (secretly / noisily) (c) The criticism was aimed squarely at the manager. (directly / accidentally) (d) The meticulous editor checked every comma. (careless / very careful) (e) She was satisfied with the result. (pleased / confused).
practice.answer: (a) briefly; (b) secretly; (c) directly; (d) very careful; (e) pleased.

practice.question: Write a short debate speech of 120–150 words either supporting or opposing the motion: “Participation of women in government should be encouraged.” State your side, give at least two reasons, support them with examples and conclude respectfully.
practice.answer: Accept either side. The speech must address the motion, give at least two relevant reasons with explanation/examples, maintain respectful language and end with a clear conclusion.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Answering comprehension questions and contextual synonyms
objectives: Explain a practical sequence for answering comprehension questions.
Answer questions from an original passage using only stated or supported information.
Choose contextual synonyms while preserving grammatical form.
lessons.body:
Comprehension is the ability to understand a passage and respond accurately to what it says. Read the instructions first so that you know whether you must answer in your own words, choose a synonym, explain a phrase or give a short summary. Skim the passage once to identify its subject and general direction. Read the questions carefully; they tell you which details to locate. Reread the relevant section slowly and check the surrounding sentences before answering. Base factual answers on the passage, not on outside knowledge or personal assumptions. If a question asks for a reason, give the reason stated or clearly supported in the text.
For a synonym question, replace the target word with a word or phrase that preserves the meaning in that sentence. Check grammar as well as meaning: a plural noun normally needs a plural substitute; a past-tense verb needs a past-tense substitute; an adjective should be replaced by an adjective where possible. Read the whole sentence with your substitute. A dictionary synonym is not automatically correct in every context. For example, “The road was costly to repair” may use expensive for costly, but costly cannot be replaced by cost in that sentence without changing its grammar.
Original practice passage: A group of students noticed that the tap near their classroom often ran dry during the afternoon. At first, some pupils carried water from home, while others waited until the next break. Their class teacher asked them to record when water was available for one week. The record showed that the tap usually worked early in the morning but stopped after many classes had filled their containers. The students discussed the problem with the school caretaker and suggested a simple timetable. The caretaker explained that the storage tank was not always full because a valve sometimes remained partly closed. After the valve was repaired, the school introduced a short schedule for filling containers. The students also agreed not to leave taps running. Within a few days, queues became shorter and less water was wasted. The class learned that careful observation, respectful discussion and shared responsibility can solve a practical problem.
When answering, distinguish a fact from an inference. “The students recorded water availability for one week” is stated. “They learned to cooperate” is supported by the final sentence. Do not claim that the school installed a new tank: the passage says that a valve was repaired.

practice.question: Answer from the passage: (a) When did the tap usually work? (b) What did the students record? (c) What did the caretaker say was wrong? (d) What change reduced waste?
practice.answer: (a) Early in the morning. (b) When water was available for one week. (c) A valve sometimes remained partly closed. (d) Repairing the valve, introducing a filling schedule and not leaving taps running.

practice.question: Give one inference supported by the passage about how the students approached the problem. Support it with a detail.
practice.answer: They approached it cooperatively and respectfully; for example, they kept a record and discussed their suggestion with the caretaker.

practice.question: Replace the bold word with a suitable synonym that keeps the grammar: (a) The queue became **shorter**. (b) The pupils **noticed** the problem. (c) They made a **simple** timetable. (d) The caretaker **explained** the fault. (e) The students **agreed** to save water.
practice.answer: Accept: (a) reduced/less long; (b) observed/spotted; (c) straightforward/easy; (d) described/made clear; (e) decided/consented. Each substitute must fit the sentence.

practice.question: State whether each statement is stated, supported by inference, or not supported: (a) The students recorded water availability for a week. (b) The school bought a new tank. (c) The class learned shared responsibility. (d) The tap stopped working after many classes had filled containers.
practice.answer: (a) stated; (b) not supported; (c) supported by inference (also stated in the final sentence); (d) stated.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Emphatic stress: contrast, correction and question matching
objectives: Define emphatic stress and explain how it changes sentence focus.
Identify how stress on different words changes the intended meaning.
Match an emphatically stressed sentence to the question it answers.
Distinguish suitable formal and informal requests in conversation.
lessons.body:
Emphatic stress is the extra force given to one word in a sentence to show a contrast, correction or important information. The sentence may keep the same word order while its meaning changes according to the word stressed. In writing, a teacher may show the stressed word in CAPITALS; in speech, the speaker gives it greater prominence.
Example sentence: “JAMES borrowed my bicycle yesterday.” Stress on JAMES corrects who borrowed it: not another person. “James BORROWED my bicycle yesterday” contrasts borrowing with buying or stealing. “James borrowed MY bicycle yesterday” contrasts my bicycle with someone else's. “James borrowed my BICYCLE yesterday” contrasts the bicycle with another object. “James borrowed my bicycle YESTERDAY” contrasts the time with another day. The listener asks what information is being corrected or contrasted.
A useful test is to match the stressed word with the question the sentence answers. If JAMES is stressed, the question is “Who borrowed my bicycle yesterday?” If BORROWED is stressed, the question is “Did James buy my bicycle yesterday?” If MY is stressed, the question is “Whose bicycle did James borrow yesterday?” If BICYCLE is stressed, the question is “What did James borrow yesterday?” If YESTERDAY is stressed, the question is “When did James borrow my bicycle?” More than one question may be possible in a real conversation; choose the best match among the options given.
Emphatic stress is also useful in polite formal and informal conversation. In a formal exchange, speakers usually choose respectful forms such as “Could you please explain the schedule?” and “I would be grateful for your help.” In an informal exchange with a friend, “Can you explain the plan?” or “Thanks for helping” may be suitable. The speaker can use stress to correct a misunderstanding without becoming rude: “I said TUESDAY, not Thursday.”

practice.question: In “JAMES sent the message this morning”, which question is best answered when JAMES carries the emphatic stress? (a) What did James send? (b) Who sent the message? (c) When was it sent? (d) Where was it sent?
practice.answer: (b) Who sent the message?

practice.question: Match the stressed word to the question: “James BORROWED my bicycle yesterday.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did James do with the bicycle? (c) Whose bicycle was it? (d) When did he borrow it?
practice.answer: (b) What did James do with the bicycle?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed MY bicycle yesterday.” (a) Whose bicycle did James borrow? (b) What did James borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Who borrowed it?
practice.answer: (a) Whose bicycle did James borrow?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed my BICYCLE yesterday.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did James borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Whose bicycle was it?
practice.answer: (b) What did James borrow?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed my bicycle YESTERDAY.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did he borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Why did he borrow it?
practice.answer: (c) When did he borrow it?

practice.question: Rewrite “I said Tuesday, not Thursday” to show the word that should receive emphatic stress to correct each misunderstanding: (a) the day was Tuesday, not another day; (b) I said it, not another person.
practice.answer: (a) I said TUESDAY, not Thursday. (b) I said Tuesday, not another person (stress I).

practice.question: Write one suitable formal request and one suitable informal request asking someone to explain a timetable. State one difference in register.
practice.answer: Accept: formal “Could you please explain the timetable?”; informal “Can you explain the timetable?” Difference: formal language is more courteous/distant; informal language is more relaxed/familiar.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 9 original revision: antonyms, word bank and informal letter
objectives: Choose context-appropriate antonyms.
Use vocabulary in context and maintain grammatical accuracy.
Write an informal letter about a verifiable civic or political change.
lessons.body:
This is an original, keyed Week 9 revision activity. It does not reproduce the unkeyed source questions or unavailable textbook assignments.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings in a particular context. Choose the opposite that fits the sentence, not simply a word that looks different. Sportsmanship is fair and respectful behaviour in a game; an antonym in context may be unsporting conduct. Cautious means careful to avoid danger; reckless is a suitable opposite. Natural means occurring in nature or not artificial; artificial is an opposite in the relevant sense. Giant means extremely large; tiny is an opposite. Conservative may mean favouring limited or gradual change; radical or reformist may be an opposite depending on context. Always use the sentence to decide.
A word bank exercise tests both meaning and grammar. Read the whole sentence, identify the missing part of speech, and use each bank word only where its meaning fits. Check whether the word needs a singular or plural form and whether the sentence remains grammatical.
An informal letter to a friend abroad has the writer's address and date, a friendly greeting, an opening that refers to the friend, clear paragraphs, a suitable closing and the writer's name. When describing political changes in your country, separate verified events from personal opinions. Give dates or names only when you are certain; avoid rumours, insults and unsupported claims. Explain why a change matters to ordinary people and invite the friend to share news from their own country.

practice.question: Choose a suitable antonym for the bold word in each context: (a) The captain showed good **sportsmanship**. (b) A **cautious** driver checks the road. (c) The flowers were **natural**, not plastic. (d) A **giant** tree shaded the field. (e) The committee rejected a **conservative** proposal and demanded radical change.
practice.answer: (a) unsporting conduct; (b) reckless; (c) artificial; (d) tiny; (e) radical or strongly reformist (in this context).

practice.question: Complete each sentence with one suitable word from this bank: secular, ethics, denomination, doctrine, pilgrimage, fanatics, worship, Bible, monotheist. (a) A person who believes in one God is a _____. (b) A journey to a sacred place for religious reasons is a _____. (c) A system of moral principles is called _____. (d) A group within a larger religion is a _____. (e) People may gather to _____ in a place of worship. (f) A state that does not favour one religion in its public institutions may be described as _____.
practice.answer: (a) monotheist; (b) pilgrimage; (c) ethics; (d) denomination; (e) worship; (f) secular. Each answer is used once; the remaining bank words are not needed.

practice.question: Write an informal letter of 150–180 words to a friend abroad describing one political or civic change you can verify in your community or country. Explain its possible effect on ordinary people, distinguish fact from opinion, and invite your friend to reply.
practice.answer: Accept a coherent informal letter with appropriate layout, one accurately described verifiable change, a reasoned explanation of its possible effects, a clear distinction between fact and opinion, and an appropriate friendly close.

marking.criterion: accurate, verifiable description of a change
distinguishes fact from opinion; no unsupported claims

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Summary writing: selecting, condensing and checking main points
objectives: Explain the purpose of a summary and distinguish main points from minor details.
Apply a five-step method to select and organise relevant information.
Write an accurate concise summary without adding unsupported information.
lessons.body:
A summary is a short account of the main information in a longer passage. It keeps the important points and removes repetition, minor examples and details that do not answer the question. A summary is not a personal opinion and must not add facts that the passage does not contain.
A reliable procedure is: (1) read the instruction and note the required focus and word limit; (2) read the whole passage to understand its subject; (3) read the questions or identify the information the task requires; (4) reread and select only the points relevant to that focus; (5) combine the points in your own clear words, then check accuracy, grammar and length. A useful note beside each selected point can help you avoid copying whole sentences.
To condense, combine related points and replace lists with accurate general terms. Do not change the meaning of a technical term, omit a necessary condition or add an explanation that the passage does not support. Avoid introductory phrases such as “The passage says that” unless the task requires them. If a word limit is given, follow it; where no limit is given, ask the teacher or use the stated classroom convention rather than assuming one universal rule.
Worked passage: The school garden began with six small beds behind the science block. At first, pupils watered them with buckets, but the work took too long and some plants dried out. The science club asked the caretaker for permission to collect rainwater from a roof gutter. They placed a covered storage drum beside the garden and used a watering can to share the water fairly. The club labelled each bed with the crop name and the date of planting. Members took turns checking the soil and removing weeds. After several weeks, the garden produced vegetables for a cooking demonstration. The project taught pupils to plan tasks, conserve water and work together.
Main points: six beds started; rainwater was collected in a covered drum; pupils shared watering and cared for labelled beds; vegetables were produced; pupils learned planning, conservation and cooperation. Model summary (35 words): “Pupils developed a school garden by collecting rainwater, sharing watering duties and caring for labelled beds. The garden produced vegetables and taught them planning, water conservation and cooperation.” This keeps the main actions and outcome without repeating minor details.

practice.question: In one sentence, define a summary and state two things it should not contain.
practice.answer: A summary is a concise account of the main relevant points in a passage. It should not contain irrelevant details or unsupported personal opinions/new facts.

marking.criterion: no unsupported opinion or added fact

practice.question: From the worked garden passage, list four main points that should appear in a summary.
practice.answer: Accept: pupils started six beds; collected rainwater in a covered drum; shared watering and cared for labelled beds; harvested vegetables; learned planning, conservation and cooperation.

practice.question: Write a summary of the worked garden passage in not more than 40 words.
practice.answer: Sample: “Pupils created a school garden by collecting rainwater, sharing watering duties and caring for labelled beds. The garden produced vegetables and taught them planning, conservation and cooperation.”

marking.criterion: includes the project and rainwater solution

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Prefixes and suffixes: meanings, word formation and spelling changes
objectives: Distinguish roots, bases, prefixes and suffixes.
Explain common prefix and suffix meanings and form words accurately.
Apply common spelling changes when adding suffixes.
Use affixes in original keyed practice.
lessons.body:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning or grammatical function in a word. An affix is a morpheme attached to a base or root. A prefix comes before the base; a suffix comes after it. The root carries the central meaning, while an affix changes or adds to that meaning or changes the word's grammatical class. Do not call every similar sequence of letters an affix: compare re- in rewrite (again) with re in reason, where the letters do not carry the prefix meaning.
Common prefixes: un- (not/opposite: unhappy); non- (not or absence: non-fiction); dis- (opposite or reversal: disagree, disconnect); mis- (wrongly: misread); mal- (badly: malfunction); super- (above or beyond: superhuman); trans- (across: transport); inter- (between: interact); post- (after: postwar); ex- (former or out of: ex-president); out- (surpass: outnumber); re- (again: rewrite); pre- (before: preview); anti- (against: anti-war); de- (reverse/remove/reduce: defrost, devalue). Some prefixes have more than one sense; check the whole word in context.
Common suffixes: -ness forms nouns from adjectives (kind → kindness); -ment forms nouns (develop → development); -ship forms nouns naming status or relationship (friend → friendship); -ation often forms nouns from verbs (inform → information); -er may name a person or thing that performs an action (teach → teacher); -ant may form a noun or adjective (assist → assistant); -less means without (hope → hopeless); -hood names a state or period (child → childhood); -ful means full of (care → careful); -able means capable of or suitable for (read → readable). The same ending can have different grammatical roles in different words, so examine its use.
Spelling changes matter. A final silent e is often dropped before a vowel-starting suffix: create → creation; admire → admirable. A final consonant may double after a short stressed vowel in some forms: begin → beginning; prefer → preferred. A final consonant plus y often changes y to i before -ness or -ment where appropriate: happy → happiness; rely → reliable. Do not apply a rule mechanically: keep the spelling of established words and check doubtful forms in a dictionary. A prefix usually attaches without changing the spelling of the base: mis + spell → misspell; dis + agree → disagree.
To analyse a word, identify the base, identify any prefix or suffix, explain the affix's contribution, and check whether the whole word's meaning matches the context. For example, unhelpful = un- (not) + help + -ful (full of/helping): not helpful. Friendship = friend + -ship, a noun naming a relationship.

practice.question: In each word, identify the prefix or suffix and give its meaning: (a) misread; (b) postwar; (c) kindness; (d) hopeless; (e) preview; (f) friendship.
practice.answer: (a) mis- = wrongly; (b) post- = after; (c) -ness = state/quality; (d) -less = without; (e) pre- = before; (f) -ship = state/relationship.

practice.question: Form a word with the requested affix: (a) happy + -ness; (b) teach + -er; (c) agree + dis-; (d) read + -able; (e) child + -hood; (f) spell + mis-.
practice.answer: (a) happiness; (b) teacher; (c) disagree; (d) readable; (e) childhood; (f) misspell.

practice.question: Explain why re- is a prefix in rewrite but not in reason. Then identify the base and affix in unhelpful.
practice.answer: In rewrite, re- means again and attaches to write; in reason, re- is not a separate morpheme with that meaning. Unhelpful = un- + help + -ful.

marking.criterion: reason is not analysed as re- + ason

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adverbial phrases and the functions of prepositional phrases
objectives: Define an adverbial phrase and identify its common meanings.
Identify manner, time, place, reason, purpose, concession and degree phrases.
Explain the adverbial, adjectival, verb-complement and adjective-complement functions of prepositional phrases.
Distinguish prepositional phrases from adverbial clauses.
lessons.body:
An adverbial phrase is a group of words without its own finite subject–verb clause that functions like an adverb. It gives information about an action or description: how, when, where, why, for what purpose, to what extent, or despite what circumstance. Examples: She answered with care (manner); We met after lunch (time); The children waited at the gate (place); Because of the rain, the match stopped (reason); They saved money for a new roof (purpose); Despite the delay, the bus arrived (concession); The room was quiet to a remarkable degree (degree). A phrase can be adverbial even when it begins with a preposition.
A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and contains its complement, usually a noun phrase or pronoun: under the table; beside the road; with her; after the lesson. The preposition relates its complement to another word or part of the sentence. A prepositional phrase may perform different functions.
(1) Adverbial function: it modifies a verb or clause and gives time, place, manner, reason or another circumstance: The team practised in the afternoon (when?); She spoke with confidence (how?). (2) Adjectival function: it modifies a noun: The house on the hill belongs to us (which house?). (3) Complement of a verb: some verbs require or naturally take a prepositional complement to complete the meaning: We depend on our neighbours; She listened to the announcement. (4) Complement of an adjective: some adjectives take a prepositional complement: They are proud of their work; I am interested in science. The same prepositional phrase can be classified by its structure (prepositional phrase) and by its function in the sentence (adverbial, adjectival or complement).
Do not confuse an adverbial phrase with an adverbial clause. “After the meeting” is a phrase because it has no subject and finite verb. “After the meeting ended” is a clause because meeting is the subject of ended. To analyse a phrase, find its beginning preposition if there is one, identify the complement, then ask what word or idea it modifies or completes.

practice.question: Identify the adverbial phrase and state whether it expresses manner, time, place, reason, purpose, concession or degree: (a) She completed the task with care. (b) We shall meet after lunch. (c) The children waited at the gate. (d) Because of the heavy rain, the match stopped. (e) Despite the delay, the bus arrived. (f) He spoke to a great extent with confidence.
practice.answer: (a) with care — manner; (b) after lunch — time; (c) at the gate — place; (d) because of the heavy rain — reason; (e) despite the delay — concession; (f) to a great extent — degree; with confidence — manner.

practice.question: For each prepositional phrase, state its function: (a) The keys are on the shelf. (b) The girl with the red scarf is my sister. (c) We rely on our neighbours. (d) They are proud of their work.
practice.answer: (a) adverbial/place complement of are; (b) adjectival modifier of girl; (c) complement of the verb rely; (d) complement of the adjective proud.

practice.question: State whether the bracketed group is a phrase or a clause: (a) [after the lesson]; (b) [after the lesson ended]. Give a structural reason for each.
practice.answer: (a) phrase: no subject and finite verb; (b) clause: lesson is the subject and ended is the finite verb.

practice.question: Write one original sentence containing an adverbial phrase of purpose and one containing a prepositional phrase that complements an adjective. Underline each phrase and label its function.
practice.answer: Accept e.g. “We saved money for a school trip” (for a school trip: purpose) and “She is interested in science” (in science: adjective complement).

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 10 original revision: phrasal verbs and contextual vocabulary
objectives: Choose suitable completions involving phrasal verbs, vocabulary and collocation.
Give context-appropriate synonyms for five target words and phrases.
lessons.body:
This is an original Week 10 revision activity with a key. It does not reproduce the source's unkeyed multiple-choice items.
Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle or preposition to create a meaning. Turn someone down means reject an offer or request: The committee turned down the proposal. Candid means honest and direct; catastrophic means disastrous; proficient means skilled; erratic means irregular or unpredictable. Choose a substitute that fits the sentence and preserves its grammatical form.
When completing a sentence, check the whole construction. A determiner comes before a noun (each student, those books); a degree word modifies an adjective or adverb (very careful); a noun names a person, place, thing or idea; and a collocation is a combination of words that commonly occur together (make a decision, heavy rain).

practice.question: Choose the best completion: (a) The committee decided to (turn down / turn up) the proposal because it was too expensive. (b) The witness gave a (candid / catastrophic) account. (c) The trained technician is (proficient / erratic) in using the equipment. (d) The storm caused (catastrophic / candid) damage. (e) The machine gives (erratic / proficient) readings.
practice.answer: (a) turn down; (b) candid; (c) proficient; (d) catastrophic; (e) erratic.

practice.question: Give a suitable synonym for each word or phrase: (a) turn him down; (b) candid; (c) catastrophic; (d) proficient; (e) erratic.
practice.answer: (a) reject/refuse; (b) frank/honest; (c) disastrous; (d) skilled/competent; (e) irregular/unpredictable.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Informal letters: layout, openings, body and closing
objectives: Explain the purpose and tone of an informal letter.
Arrange address, date, salutation, opening, body, close and name in an accepted layout.
Choose suitable greetings and closings for a familiar recipient.
Write considerate personal advice while respecting the recipient's autonomy.
lessons.body:
An informal letter is a personal message to someone with whom the writer has a familiar relationship, such as a relative or friend. It uses a warm, natural tone but should still be clear, organised and respectful. Read the question carefully and answer every part of it; a friendly tone does not excuse ignoring the task.
The writer's address is placed at the top right or in the position required by the school's accepted layout. Write the date below it. Do not include a recipient's address in a typical informal letter unless the task or teacher specifically requests it. The salutation is the greeting, for example “Dear Amina,” “Dear Mum,” or “My dear Uncle,”. Choose a form that suits the relationship; capitalise the name or relationship title and use a comma after the greeting.
The opening may acknowledge a letter received, ask after the person's health or introduce the reason for writing. For example: “Thank you for your letter, which I received last week. I hope you and the family are well.” The body should follow the exact instruction in the question. Organise it into paragraphs, one main idea at a time. Give advice with reasons rather than commands, and avoid insulting or blaming the recipient. If the task asks you to advise a sister about a serious family decision, show concern, encourage her to consider safety and seek trusted support, and respect that the decision is hers; do not pressure someone to remain in an unsafe relationship.
The closing sentence may express affection, good wishes or an invitation to reply. A complimentary close for a familiar recipient might be “With love,” “Yours affectionately,” or “Your loving brother,”. Choose one that matches the relationship and remain consistent with the writer's identity. Place the close at the lower right in the layout used by the school, then write the name by which the recipient knows the writer. A signature is optional for a personal letter and is not a substitute for the writer's name.
A simple plan is: address and date; salutation; friendly opening; paragraphs that answer the question; friendly closing sentence; complimentary close and name. Check that the letter has the correct tone, complete task coverage, paragraphing, punctuation and accurate language.

practice.question: Name six parts or features of an informal letter in the order in which they normally appear.
practice.answer: Writer's address, date, salutation, opening/introduction, body, closing sentence, complimentary close and writer's name (any six in correct order).

marking.criterion: six valid features in correct order

practice.question: Choose a suitable salutation and complimentary close for a letter to your sister. Explain one reason for each choice.
practice.answer: Accept “Dear Amina,” or “My dear Sister,” and “With love,” or “Yours affectionately,” with a reason that the wording suits a familiar relationship.

practice.question: Write the opening paragraph of an informal letter to a friend who sent you news last week. Acknowledge the letter and ask after the friend.
practice.answer: Accept any natural, polite opening that acknowledges the letter and asks after the friend.

practice.question: State two ways to make advice in a personal letter respectful rather than controlling.
practice.answer: Examples: give reasons; use considerate language; recognise the recipient's right to decide; encourage trusted support; avoid insults, threats or commands.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Articles: a, an, the and zero article
objectives: Distinguish definite and indefinite articles and zero article.
Choose a or an according to the initial sound.
Use the for identifiable, unique, specific and generic references where appropriate.
Apply article rules to singular, plural and non-count nouns.
lessons.body:
Articles are determiners used before nouns. English has two indefinite articles, a and an, and one definite article, the. English also uses a zero article (no article) in many general statements and before some names and plural or non-count nouns.
Use a before a singular count noun that begins with a consonant sound: a book, a uniform, a European city, a university, a one-way street. The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter. Use an before a singular count noun that begins with a vowel sound: an apple, an egg, an hour, an honest person, an honour. The h is silent in hour, honest and honour, so the next sound is a vowel. In house, home and hoe, h is pronounced, so use a house, a home and a hoe. The same sound rule applies to abbreviations: an MBA student (the letter name begins with a vowel sound), a UN meeting (you begins with /j/).
Use the before a noun when the speaker and listener can identify the particular person or thing: Please close the door; the bag under the chair is mine. Use it for something unique in the relevant context: the sun, the moon, the principal of our school. Use the with a singular noun to represent a whole class in a general statement when that pattern is natural: The tiger is a powerful animal. Plural and non-count nouns can be used without an article for general meaning: Tigers are mammals; Water is essential. Use the when the reference is specific: The water in this bottle is cold; the tigers in that enclosure are resting.
Use a or an when introducing one non-specific singular count noun for the first time: I saw a bird. Use the when referring to it again: The bird landed on a wall. A/an cannot normally be used with a plural count noun or a non-count noun: say some books or books, not “a books”; say advice or some advice, not “an advice”.
The may be used with certain names of newspapers and organisations when it forms part of their established title, such as The Guardian or The Times. Follow the official styling of the name. Do not add the automatically to every institution, office or country name. Use the with adjectives to refer to a whole group of people: the rich, the poor, the elderly. These expressions take a plural verb when they refer to people as a group: The elderly are entitled to respect.
Zero article is common with plural and non-count nouns when speaking generally, languages and school subjects, and many proper names: Children need sleep; She studies English; We visited Ibadan. Compare specific reference: The children in our class need sleep; the English in this passage is formal. Article choice depends on countability, sound and whether the reference is general, first-mentioned or already identifiable.

practice.question: Insert a, an, the or Ø (no article): (a) She studies ___ English. (b) He waited for ___ hour. (c) We saw ___ university near the station. (d) Please close ___ window beside you. (e) ___ water is essential for life. (f) ___ water in this bottle is cold.
practice.answer: (a) Ø; (b) an; (c) a; (d) the; (e) Ø; (f) the.

practice.question: Choose the correct article: (a) a/an honest person; (b) a/an uniform; (c) a/an MBA student; (d) a/an house; (e) a/an European country.
practice.answer: (a) an; (b) a; (c) an; (d) a; (e) a.

practice.question: Explain the difference in meaning: (a) “I bought a book” and “I read the book”; (b) “Books are useful” and “The books on the desk are mine.”
practice.answer: (a) a book introduces one non-specific book; the book refers to an identifiable book already mentioned. (b) Books means books generally; the books on the desk identifies a particular set.

practice.question: Correct the article errors and explain the rule: (a) She is an university student. (b) I need an advice. (c) The children need the sleep in general.
practice.answer: (a) She is a university student (university begins with /j/ consonant sound). (b) I need advice/some advice (advice is non-count). (c) Children need sleep in general (zero article for general plural and non-count nouns).

marking.criterion: (a) corrects to a and gives sound rule
(b) removes an and recognises non-count noun

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Consonant sounds and spelling patterns: /b d k f g dʒ h/
objectives: Identify the articulation place and manner of /b/, /d/ and /k/.
Recognise common spelling patterns for /b/, /d/, /k/, /f/, /g/, /dʒ/ and /h/.
Distinguish phonemes from letter spellings and avoid common spelling generalisations.
lessons.body:
A consonant sound is produced with some narrowing or closure in the vocal tract. The following notes use broad British English IPA. A phoneme is a sound, while letters and letter groups are spellings; one sound may have several spellings, and one spelling may represent different sounds in different words.
/b/ is a voiced bilabial plosive: both lips close and release with vocal-fold vibration. Common spellings include b (bag, table) and bb (rabbit, ribbon). /d/ is a voiced alveolar plosive: the tongue tip or blade contacts the alveolar ridge. Common spellings include d (day, ladder) and dd (middle); the regular past-tense ending -ed is pronounced /d/ after many voiced sounds, as in played and cleaned.
/k/ is a voiceless velar plosive: the back of the tongue contacts the soft palate. Common spellings include c (cat, cold), k (kite, skin), ck (back, ticket) and ch in some words of Greek origin (school, chemistry, character). /f/ is a voiceless labiodental fricative: the lower lip approaches the upper teeth. Spellings include f (fan), ff (coffee), ph (phone) and gh in some words (laugh, cough). The letter v normally represents /v/, not /f/: van begins with /v/, so do not treat v as a general spelling of /f/.
/g/ is a voiced velar plosive, as in go and bigger. It is commonly spelled g and gg; gh represents /g/ in a small number of words such as ghost and ghastly, but gh is silent or represents other sounds in many other words. /dʒ/ is a voiced postalveolar affricate, as in jam. Common spellings include j (jam), g before e, i or y (giant, gentle, gym), dge (bridge) and dg in a few words (adjudge). The symbol is /dʒ/, not /dz/.
/h/ is a voiceless glottal fricative, as in hat and ahead. It is usually spelled h. The spelling wh represents /h/ in a few words such as who and whose in many accents, but represents /w/ in where and when. Always check the pronunciation of the word rather than assuming that every wh has the same sound.
When identifying an odd word, state the sound or spelling pattern that makes it different. A spelling group may be shared by words that do not all contain the same sound; use the target sound, not only the letters, as your criterion. These are spelling and phoneme notes, not a substitute for listening assessment; no audio model is supplied in this lesson.

practice.question: Give the consonant sound represented by the first bold letter group: (a) **b**ag; (b) **d**ay; (c) **c**at; (d) **ph**one; (e) **j**am; (f) **h**at.

Choose the word in which the bold spelling represents the target sound: (a) /f/: **ph** in phone or **v** in van; (b) /k/: **ch** in school or **ch** in chair; (c) /dʒ/: **g** in giant or **g** in goat; (d) /h/: **wh** in who or **wh** in when.
practice.answer: (a) phone; (b) school; (c) giant; (d) who.

practice.question: State the place and manner of articulation for /b/, /d/ and /k/.
practice.answer: /b/: bilabial plosive; /d/: alveolar plosive; /k/: velar plosive.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 11 original revision: sentence completion and contextual vocabulary
objectives: Choose correct forms and collocations in sentence-completion items.
Select context-appropriate synonyms.
lessons.body:
This original revision set provides its own answer key; it does not reuse the source's unkeyed exercises.
Choose the word that best completes each sentence by checking grammar, meaning and collocation. “Whose” asks about possession; “who's” means who is or who has. “Unless” means if not. “About” may introduce a topic. “Make it” can mean arrive or succeed. “If and when” refers to a possible event and its timing.
Nearest-in-meaning questions require a substitute that fits the context. For example, a person who is competent is capable or skilled; an expression may have a different meaning in another sentence, so read the whole context before choosing.
For a two-word choice, check the grammatical structure around the blank and read the complete sentence aloud. A correct option must fit both meaning and syntax.

practice.question: Choose the best completion: (a) (Whose/Who's) notebook is this? (b) You will not improve (unless/about) you practise. (c) We talked (about/unless) the new timetable. (d) I hope you can (make it/make up) to the meeting. (e) We will begin (if and when/whose) the guests arrive.
practice.answer: (a) Whose; (b) unless; (c) about; (d) make it; (e) if and when.

practice.question: Give a suitable synonym for each word: (a) competent; (b) reluctant; (c) frequent.
practice.answer: (a) capable/skilled; (b) unwilling/hesitant; (c) often/repeated.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Affixes, roots and word formation across word classes
objectives: Define morpheme, affix, affixation, root and base and explain their relationships.
Identify common prefixes and explain their meanings with accurate examples.
Identify suffixes that form adjectives, nouns and verbs.
Apply common spelling changes when adding suffixes.
Use affix analysis to form and interpret words accurately.
lessons.body:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning or grammatical function in a word. An affix is a morpheme attached to a base or root; affixation is the process of adding an affix. A prefix comes before the base, while a suffix comes after it. A root is the central element carrying the core meaning. A base is the form to which an affix is attached; a base may itself contain more than one morpheme. For example, in unhappy, happy is the base and root, and un- is a prefix. In happiness, happy is the base and -ness is a suffix. Do not force a split where no meaningful affix is present: welcome is not formed from come with a prefix wel-, and comedy is not come plus -dy.
Common prefixes from the source table, with accurate examples: a- can mean not (atypical, amoral); ab- means away or from (abduct, abnormal); ante- means before (antenatal, antecedent); anti- means against (antivirus, antiwar); con-/com- means with or together (connect, combine); de- can mean reverse, remove or reduce (defrost, deactivate); di- means two (dioxide, diatomic); en-/em- means cause to be or put into (enrich, empower); bi- means two (bicycle, bilingual); ex- can mean out of (export, exhale) or former (ex-president); fore- means before or ahead (forecast, foretell); hyper- means excessive or above normal (hyperactive, hypertension); inter- means between (international, interact). Meanings depend on the word; use a dictionary when unsure.
Other common prefixes useful in school vocabulary include dis- (opposite or reversal: disagree), il-/im-/in-/ir- (not: illegal, impossible, inactive, irregular), mis- (wrongly: misread), non- (not: non-fiction), pre- (before: preview), pro- (in favour of: pro-democracy), re- (again: rewrite), sub- (under: submarine), super- (above or beyond: superhuman), tele- (at a distance: telephone), trans- (across: transport), tri- (three: triangle) and uni- (one: uniform). These are additional examples, not an assumption that every unclear fragment in the source list is a prefix. “Mat” and “ploy” are not treated as independent prefixes in this lesson; the teacher should confirm whether the source assignment has been truncated or mistyped.
Suffixes can form different word classes. Adjective-forming suffixes include -able/-ible (readable, visible), -ful (hopeful), -less (careless), -ish (childish), -ous (dangerous), -ic (historic), -like (childlike), -y (rainy), -en (wooden) and -ly in adjectives such as friendly and lively. Noun-forming suffixes include -er/-or/-ar (teacher, actor, beggar), -ship (friendship), -hood (childhood), -ness (kindness), -ance/-ence (attendance, difference), -ism (realism), -dom (freedom), -tion/-sion (education, decision), -ity (activity), -ure (failure) and -ment (punishment). Verb-forming suffixes include -ise/-ize (nationalise/nationalize), -en (widen, strengthen), -ify (simplify) and -ate (activate). Some endings have more than one use; check the word's grammatical role in context.
The endings -ing and -ed commonly mark verb forms (walking, walked) and may also form adjectives (a boring lesson, a tired pupil). They are grammatical endings in many uses, not proof that a new dictionary word has been formed. The source's forms -any, -evy, -ude and -em are not taught as productive English suffixes because they are not reliable suffix entries in the stated roles.
Spelling changes when suffixes are added: happy → happiness (y changes to i); rely → reliable (y changes to i); create → creation (silent e is dropped); hope → hopeful (silent e is usually retained before -ful); begin → beginning (final consonant doubles after a short stressed vowel in this pattern). Check individual words rather than applying a rule blindly.
To analyse a derived word, identify the base, locate the affix, state its contribution and check the resulting word class. Example: nationalise = nation + -al (adjective) + -ise (verb); nationalisation adds -ation to the verb to form a noun.

practice.question: In each word, identify the base and affix, and state whether the affix is a prefix or suffix: (a) unhappy; (b) kindness; (c) rewrite; (d) friendship; (e) impossible.
practice.answer: (a) happy + un- (prefix); (b) kind + -ness (suffix); (c) write + re- (prefix); (d) friend + -ship (suffix); (e) possible + im- (prefix).

practice.question: Give the meaning of the prefix in each word: (a) antiwar; (b) interschool; (c) forecast; (d) deactivate; (e) hyperactive; (f) bilingual.
practice.answer: (a) against; (b) between; (c) before/ahead; (d) reverse/remove activity; (e) excessive/above normal; (f) two.

practice.question: Form a word with the requested suffix: (a) kind + -ness; (b) danger + -ous; (c) nation + -al; (d) friend + -ship; (e) punish + -ment; (f) national + -ise.
practice.answer: (a) kindness; (b) dangerous; (c) national; (d) friendship; (e) punishment; (f) nationalise (or nationalize).

practice.question: Explain why welcome should not be divided into come plus a prefix wel-, and state the difference between a root and an affix.
practice.answer: Welcome is not synchronically formed by adding a meaningful prefix wel- to come; wel- has no productive prefix meaning here. A root carries the central lexical meaning; an affix is a bound morpheme added to a base/root.

marking.criterion: recognises wel- is not a meaningful prefix in welcome

practice.question: Classify each ending in the example as adjective-forming, noun-forming or verb-forming: (a) -ous in dangerous; (b) -ness in kindness; (c) -ise in nationalise; (d) -ship in friendship; (e) -able in readable.
practice.answer: (a) adjective; (b) noun; (c) verb; (d) noun; (e) adjective.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Family wellbeing: comprehension, vocabulary, linking words and summary
objectives: Read an original passage on home, family life and health and retrieve stated details.
Make inferences supported by passage evidence.
Explain seven vocabulary items in context.
Use result/addition/sequence linkers and distinguish them from apparently.
Use reporting verbs accurately.
Write a six-sentence summary using relevant points and original wording.
lessons.body:
Original comprehension passage: A Family Health Plan
The Bello family decided to make small changes to improve daily life at home. Their first endeavour was to keep a weekly record of meals, sleep and outdoor activity. Their youngest child had been afflicted by a recurring stomach ailment, so the family asked a qualified health worker for guidance rather than relying on rumours. The nurse explained that safe water, clean food, handwashing and suitable rest were important habits. She advised them to seek medical attention when symptoms were serious or persistent.
The family found that preparing balanced meals helped everyone concentrate during school and work. They included vegetables, beans, fruit and clean drinking water in their routine. The nurse explained that nutrition supports normal growth and the body's restoration after ordinary activity, while no single food prevents every illness. She also asked the family to adhere to safe food-storage practices and to keep the cooking area clean.
The parents observed that a short walk together after school made it easier to spend time as a family. They agreed that children should have enough sleep and that adults should make time for rest. Consequently, the family created a simple weekly plan. Furthermore, they placed a clean water container where everyone could reach it and agreed to wash their hands before preparing or eating food. Finally, they reviewed the plan each weekend and adjusted it when school or work commitments changed. The family learned that steady, practical habits and appropriate professional advice can support wellbeing.
Comprehension method: read the instructions; skim the passage for its subject; read the questions; reread the relevant section carefully; answer from the passage only. Distinguish a stated fact from an inference and do not add outside medical claims. A synonym must fit the sentence and preserve grammatical form.
Vocabulary in context: endeavour means a serious attempt or effort; afflicted means affected by a problem or illness; ailment means an illness or health problem; concentrating means giving close attention; adhere means follow or keep to a rule; restoration means returning something to a better or usual condition; nutrition means the process of obtaining and using food for health and growth. These are general meanings illustrated by the original passage, not claims about an unavailable textbook passage.
Summary writing: identify the question's focus, select only relevant points, combine related ideas, write in your own words and check accuracy and length. If asked for six sentences, write six complete sentences; do not add a seventh sentence as a heading or introduction. Keep one main point in each sentence where possible.
Linking words connect ideas. Consequently signals a result; furthermore adds another point; finally marks the last step or point. Apparently is an adverb meaning that something seems to be true based on available evidence; it is not a result linker like consequently. Reporting verbs introduce what a person said or communicated: noted (mentioned or recorded), observed (noticed), explained (made clear) and maintained (continued to state or defend a position). Choose the reporting verb that accurately describes the source's action.
Model six-sentence summary: The Bello family recorded their daily habits and sought qualified guidance about a recurring health problem. The nurse recommended safe water, clean food, handwashing and adequate rest. The family prepared balanced meals to support growth and concentration. They followed safe food-storage practices and kept the cooking area clean. They added family walks and agreed on suitable sleep and rest. They reviewed their plan regularly and adjusted it to their commitments.

practice.question: Answer from the passage: (a) What was the family's first endeavour? (b) Who gave them guidance? (c) Name two habits recommended by the nurse. (d) What did the family do each weekend?
practice.answer: (a) Keep a weekly record of meals, sleep and outdoor activity. (b) A nurse/qualified health worker. (c) Any two: safe water, clean food, handwashing, suitable rest, safe food storage. (d) Reviewed and adjusted the plan.

practice.question: Give one inference about why the family reviewed its plan each weekend. Support your answer with a detail from the passage.
practice.answer: They wanted the plan to remain practical as commitments changed; the passage says they adjusted it when school or work commitments changed.

practice.question: Give a suitable synonym for each word as used in the passage: (a) endeavour; (b) afflicted; (c) ailment; (d) adhere; (e) restoration; (f) concentrating; (g) nutrition.
practice.answer: (a) effort/attempt; (b) affected; (c) illness/condition; (d) follow/keep to; (e) recovery/renewal; (f) focusing; (g) nourishment/food-related process.

marking.criterion: each of seven suitable contextual meanings

practice.question: Classify each expression: consequently, furthermore, finally, apparently. Which three are used as linking expressions in the lesson, and what relationship does each signal?
practice.answer: Consequently = result; furthermore = addition; finally = final step/point; apparently = adverb meaning seemingly/on available evidence, not a result linker. The first three are the linking expressions taught.

practice.question: Write a six-sentence summary of the passage. Include the family's initial action, professional advice, food and hygiene, rest/activity and review of the plan.
practice.answer: Use the six-sentence model in the lesson as a guide. Accept equivalent accurate summaries that include all requested points, omit minor details and add no unsupported facts.

marking.criterion: six clear accurate sentences in own words

practice.question: Choose the most accurate reporting verb: (a) The nurse _____ that handwashing was important. (explained/observed) (b) The parents _____ that the walk helped them spend time together. (observed/maintained) (c) The family _____ to follow the plan. (maintained/observed).
practice.answer: (a) explained; (b) observed; (c) maintained.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Formal letters: purpose, layout, model and community request
objectives: Explain the purpose and tone of a formal letter.
Arrange sender and recipient addresses, date, salutation, subject heading, body and close.
Develop a formal request with relevant reasons and a respectful conclusion.
Write a formal letter requesting community amenities with appropriate structure.
lessons.body:
A formal letter is written to an organisation or person in an official role to make a request, complaint, recommendation or representation. Its tone is respectful, clear and purposeful. Unlike an informal letter, it normally follows a formal layout and avoids slang, personal chat and emotional exaggeration.
A common full-block layout places the sender's address and date at the top right or flush left according to the institution's style. The recipient's name or official title and address follow on the left. Use a suitable salutation: “Dear Sir,” or “Dear Madam,” when the name is unknown; use the recipient's title and surname when known. A subject heading states the purpose in a short phrase, for example “REQUEST FOR COMMUNITY AMENITIES”. The body opens by identifying the writer or group and stating the purpose. Each following paragraph develops one request and explains its practical reason. The final paragraph states the action requested and thanks the recipient for considering it. Close with “Yours faithfully,” when the recipient is addressed as Sir or Madam; “Yours sincerely,” is normally used when the recipient is addressed by name. Add the writer's name and role where relevant.
Model letter:
12 Unity Road,
Adebayo Community,
Ibadan.
7 November 2026.
The Chairperson,
Community Development Council,
Adebayo Community.
Dear Madam,
REQUEST FOR COMMUNITY AMENITIES
I am writing on behalf of residents of Adebayo Community to request your consideration of three improvements that would make the area safer and healthier.
First, residents would benefit from reliable street lighting along the main footpaths. Better lighting would help people move safely after dusk and may discourage vandalism. We ask the Council to assess the most urgent locations and advise residents on a realistic installation plan.
Second, additional public waste bins and a regular collection schedule would help keep shared spaces clean. Residents are willing to support a community clean-up, but suitable collection arrangements are also needed to prevent refuse from accumulating.
Third, we request that the Council liaise with the relevant health authorities about access to a nearby primary health service. This would help families understand where to obtain basic care and reliable health information.
We would be grateful if these requests could be discussed at the next community meeting. Thank you for considering the needs of residents. We would welcome an opportunity to provide further details.
Yours faithfully,
Amina Bello
Secretary, Residents' Committee

The model is an original example. It makes requests rather than claiming that a public body has already approved or funded the work. In an examination response, answer the exact question, develop reasons, use accurate facts and keep the letter within the requested length.

practice.question: State the purpose of a formal letter and give four features that distinguish it from an informal letter.
practice.answer: A formal letter communicates officially with an organisation or person in authority. Features include formal tone, recipient address, subject heading, structured paragraphs, formal salutation/close and no slang or personal chat.

practice.question: List the main parts of a formal letter in order, from sender's address to signature/name.
practice.answer: Sender's address; date; recipient's name/title and address; salutation; subject heading; opening/purpose; developed body paragraphs; closing request/thanks; complimentary close; writer's name/signature and role.

marking.criterion: five or more correct parts in correct order

practice.question: Give two reasons for each of the following community requests: street lighting, waste collection and access to a primary health service.
practice.answer: Accept relevant, practical reasons: lighting improves visibility/safety; waste collection reduces litter/pests/blocked drains; access to primary health service supports timely advice and basic care.

marking.criterion: two relevant reasons for waste collection
two relevant reasons for health access

practice.question: Write a formal subject heading and a suitable salutation and complimentary close for a letter to a chairperson whose personal name is unknown.
practice.answer: Subject: REQUEST FOR COMMUNITY AMENITIES (or similar). Salutation: Dear Sir/Madam. Close: Yours faithfully.

practice.question: Write one developed paragraph requesting a public waste collection arrangement. Include a clear request and two supporting reasons.
practice.answer: Accept a formal paragraph with a specific request and two relevant reasons such as cleanliness, reducing pests, preventing blocked drains or protecting shared spaces.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Time, tense and selected verb structures
objectives: Distinguish time as a concept from tense as a grammatical system.
Review six common English tense forms and their uses.
Form and use the present perfect continuous tense.
Use indirect questions, hypothetical conditionals, wish clauses and would-like-it-if structures accurately.
lessons.body:
Time and tense are related but not identical. Time is a concept: events may be located in the past, present or future. Tense is a grammatical form of a verb used to express a time relationship. Languages do not all organise tense in the same way. English commonly contrasts present and past verb forms; future time is often expressed with will, be going to, the present continuous or the simple present, depending on meaning and context.
The six forms reviewed here are simple present, simple past, present perfect, past perfect, present continuous and present perfect continuous. Simple present describes habits, general truths and regular occupations: She works at a clinic. Simple past describes a completed event at a past time: She worked yesterday. Present perfect uses have/has + past participle and links a past event to the present: She has completed the report. It is not normally used with a finished definite past-time expression such as yesterday; use the simple past instead. Past perfect uses had + past participle for an event earlier than another past event: She had left before the bus arrived. Present continuous uses am/is/are + -ing for an action in progress or a temporary arrangement: She is studying now. Present perfect continuous uses have/has been + -ing for an activity that began earlier and continues to the present, or has a present result: She has been studying for two hours; It has been raining, so the ground is wet.
Two examples each: Present continuous: “The pupils are writing their notes.” “I am waiting for the bus.” Present perfect continuous: “We have been practising since Monday.” “He has been working here for three years.” Past perfect: “The guests had eaten before the film began.” “She had finished the task when the bell rang.”
Indirect questions are embedded questions and use statement word order: “Could you tell me where the office is?” not “Could you tell me where is the office?” Unreal or hypothetical conditionals commonly use if + past form for an imagined present/future situation and would + base verb in the result: “If I had more time, I would read every day.” With be, “If I were you” is a common formal hypothetical form. Wish + past form can express regret about a present situation: “I wish I knew the answer.” “Would like it if” can express a polite preference: “I would like it if you arrived on time.” These structures must be interpreted by context; the past form does not always mean past time.

practice.question: Choose the correct form: (a) She (works/has worked) here every day as part of her regular job. (b) We (visited/have visited) the museum yesterday. (c) They (had left/have left) before the rain started. (d) He (is reading/reads) at the moment. (e) I (have been waiting/wait) for an hour and I am still here.
practice.answer: (a) works; (b) visited; (c) had left; (d) is reading; (e) have been waiting.

practice.question: Correct the word order in each indirect question: (a) Could you tell me where is the library? (b) Do you know when does the meeting begin?
practice.answer: (a) Could you tell me where the library is? (b) Do you know when the meeting begins?

practice.question: Complete each hypothetical sentence: (a) If I were the chairperson, I _____ (improve) the road. (b) I wish I _____ (know) the answer. (c) I would like it if you _____ (arrive) on time.
practice.answer: (a) would improve; (b) knew; (c) arrived.

practice.question: Write two original examples each of the present continuous, present perfect continuous and past perfect. Underline the verb phrase in each sentence.
practice.answer: Accept six grammatical examples with correct forms: am/is/are + -ing; have/has been + -ing; had + past participle.

marking.criterion: two correct present perfect continuous examples

practice.question: Explain the difference between time and tense in two or three sentences.
practice.answer: Time is the conceptual location of an event (past, present or future); tense is a grammatical verb form or system used by a language to express time relationships.

marking.criterion: time defined as conceptual event location
tense defined as grammatical verb form/system

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Synonyms, picture words and meaning in context
objectives: Define synonyms and distinguish exact from near synonyms.
Distinguish painting, drawing, portrait, print and sketch while recognising overlap.
Choose among arrange, organise and plan in context.
Explain multiple meanings of hide, great, funny, floor and fabric.
Use context to choose and demonstrate accurate word meanings.
lessons.body:
A synonym is a word or expression with the same or a similar meaning to another word in a particular context. Exact synonyms are uncommon because words often differ in tone, register, grammar or the situations in which they are used. Near synonyms overlap in meaning but are not always interchangeable. Odour, smell and scent all refer to something detected by the nose, but odour may sound neutral or unpleasant, smell is general, and scent often suggests a pleasant or noticeable smell. Read the whole sentence before choosing a synonym.
Picture is a broad word for a visual representation of a person, scene or thing. A painting is an image made by applying paint to a surface. A drawing is made with lines, usually using pencil, pen, charcoal or another drawing tool. A portrait is an image of a person, often focusing on the face or upper body; it may be a painting, drawing, photograph or digital image. A print is a copy produced by printing or reproducing an image, often from a photograph or original artwork. A sketch is a quick, simple drawing that records an idea or outline without many details. These words overlap: a portrait can also be a painting or a drawing, and a sketch can be a preliminary drawing for a painting.
Arrange means put things in a particular order or position: arrange the chairs in rows. Organise means plan or manage people, materials or activities so that they work effectively: organise a school event. Plan means decide in advance what should happen and how to achieve it: plan a journey. The words may overlap, but their focus differs: planning decides what to do; organising manages the resources or activity; arranging places or orders particular things.
Words can have several meanings. Hide can mean put something where it cannot be seen (hide a key), or an animal's skin (a leather hide). Great can mean very good (a great idea), large or important (a great distance, a great leader). Funny can mean amusing (a funny story) or strange/unusual (a funny noise). Floor can mean the surface people walk on (clean the floor), a level of a building (the second floor), or the lowest level of something (a price floor). Fabric means cloth or material used for making clothes, curtains or other items; it can also refer figuratively to the basic structure of society. Use context to identify the intended sense.
When answering a vocabulary question, first identify the word's part of speech and role in the sentence. Then choose a meaning that fits the surrounding words. For a sentence-writing task, make the intended meaning clear through context rather than repeating the definition.

practice.question: Explain the difference between an exact synonym and a near synonym. Give one example of two near synonyms and explain a difference in their use.
practice.answer: Exact synonyms have the same meaning and are interchangeable in the relevant context, though they are rare. Near synonyms have overlapping meanings but may differ in tone or context. Example: scent often suggests a pleasant smell, while odour can be neutral or unpleasant.

practice.question: Choose the best word: (a) A quick rough picture made before a painting is a (portrait/sketch/print). (b) An image of a person's head and shoulders is often a (portrait/floor/fabric). (c) An image made with paint is a (painting/drawing/print). (d) A reproduced copy of an image may be a (print/sketch/portrait).
practice.answer: (a) sketch; (b) portrait; (c) painting; (d) print.

practice.question: Choose arrange, organise or plan: (a) We must _____ the chairs in a circle. (b) The students will _____ a fundraising event. (c) Let us _____ our revision timetable before the examination.
practice.answer: (a) arrange; (b) organise; (c) plan.

practice.question: Give the meaning of the bold word in each sentence: (a) The comedian told a **funny** story. (b) There was a **funny** smell in the room. (c) The builders reached the top **floor**. (d) The tailor selected a strong **fabric**. (e) The farmer sold an animal **hide**.
practice.answer: (a) amusing; (b) strange/unusual; (c) level/storey of a building; (d) cloth/material; (e) animal skin.

practice.question: Write one original sentence for each of these words, using a different sense from the one in the lesson's first example: hide, great, funny, floor, fabric.
practice.answer: Accept five grammatical sentences that make the intended alternate sense clear. Examples: hide the document; a great distance; a funny noise; the second floor; the fabric of society.

marking.criterion: five clear context sentences showing valid senses

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Reading for facts: scanning and supported inference
objectives: Explain scanning and distinguish it from skimming.
Locate names, dates, numbers, places and other stated facts in an original passage.
Distinguish direct facts from supported inferences.
Answer original comprehension questions accurately without adding unsupported details.
lessons.body:
Reading for facts means locating information that a passage states directly. Scanning is a quick reading technique used to find a particular name, date, number, place or stated fact. Before scanning, know what you are looking for. Let your eyes move quickly over the text, using headings, capital letters, dates, repeated terms and number patterns as clues. When you find a likely answer, read the surrounding sentence carefully to confirm it. Scanning is different from skimming: skimming gives a general idea of the whole passage, while scanning searches for a specific detail.
Original passage: A Community Bridge Project
The residents of Oke-Ayo began discussing a damaged footbridge in March 2025. The bridge crossed a narrow stream and connected the market road to the community clinic. During the rainy season, the old wooden surface became slippery, so the residents asked the local works office to inspect it. An engineer visited on 18 April and recommended replacing three damaged support beams and adding a handrail on both sides.
The community committee agreed to provide labour for clearing the approach paths, while the works office supplied treated timber and metal fittings. Repairs began on 6 May and were completed on 22 May. The total project cost was recorded as 1.8 million naira. A notice at the market listed the work schedule and the contact person, Mrs Ekanem, who received residents' questions.
After the repairs, the committee asked users to keep the bridge clear and report loose fittings. Traders said that the safer route made it easier to carry goods to the market, while clinic staff said visitors could cross more confidently. The committee planned an inspection every three months, with the first review scheduled for 22 August 2025. The project showed how residents and public workers could share responsibilities when a local facility needed repair.
To answer questions, identify whether the task asks for a direct fact or an inference. A direct fact can be found in the text, such as the completion date. An inference is a reasonable conclusion supported by one or more facts, such as the bridge being important to access essential services. Do not invent a budget source, engineering detail or official approval that the passage does not state.

practice.question: Scan the passage and give the exact facts: (a) the month residents began discussing the bridge; (b) the date the engineer visited; (c) the number of support beams to replace; (d) the date repairs began; (e) the date repairs were completed; (f) the recorded project cost; (g) the date of the first planned inspection.
practice.answer: (a) March 2025; (b) 18 April; (c) three; (d) 6 May; (e) 22 May; (f) 1.8 million naira; (g) 22 August 2025.

practice.question: Name two places connected by the bridge and the two materials supplied by the works office.
practice.answer: The market road and the community clinic; treated timber and metal fittings.

practice.question: Give one inference about why the bridge mattered to residents and support it with a detail from the passage.
practice.answer: It provided access to important community services and trade; it connected the market road and clinic, and traders carried goods across it.

practice.question: Explain the difference between skimming and scanning. Give one example of a scanning target from the passage.
practice.answer: Skimming is quick reading for general meaning; scanning is quick searching for a specific detail. Examples: 18 April, Mrs Ekanem, 1.8 million naira or 22 August 2025.

practice.question: State whether each statement is directly stated or inferred: (a) the bridge crossed a narrow stream; (b) the repairs improved access to the clinic; (c) the works office supplied the labour; (d) the committee planned inspections every three months.
practice.answer: (a) directly stated; (b) inference supported by the connection to the clinic and safer crossing; (c) not stated/false: residents supplied labour; the works office supplied materials; (d) directly stated.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Religion vocabulary in context: neutral definitions and distinctions
objectives: Define and distinguish monotheist, polytheist, atheist and agnostic.
Explain principle, doctrine, dogma, worship and ritual in context.
Explain apostasy, ablution, immersion and confirmation using neutral examples.
Use religion-related vocabulary accurately and respectfully.
lessons.body:
This lesson explains religion-related vocabulary neutrally for language study. It describes how words are used; it does not promote or criticise any religion or belief.
A spirit may refer to a non-physical being or presence in a religious or cultural belief, or to a person's courage and energy in expressions such as team spirit. Gods is the plural of god and is used when a belief system refers to more than one deity. A monotheist believes in one God; a polytheist believes in more than one god. An atheist does not believe that any god exists. An agnostic considers that the existence of a god or gods is unknown or may be unknowable. These terms describe different positions and should not be used as insults.
A principle is a basic rule, belief or value that guides behaviour. A doctrine is a set of teachings or beliefs held by a group or tradition. Dogma is a belief or teaching presented as authoritative and not open to question by those who accept it; the word can carry a critical tone. Worship is the act of showing reverence or devotion to a deity or sacred object, often through prayer, song or ceremony. A ritual is an established series of actions performed in a particular order, often for cultural or religious reasons.
Apostasy means formally abandoning or renouncing a religious faith or allegiance. Ablution means washing, especially as a religious preparation or act of purification in some traditions. Immersion means putting something completely under a liquid; in some religious contexts it describes a ceremony in which a person is immersed in water. Confirmation has several meanings: proof that something is true, or in some Christian traditions a ceremony recognising or strengthening a person's membership in the church. The exact sense depends on the sentence and tradition being discussed.
Use a neutral sentence to show meaning: “The historian compared the doctrines of two traditions.” “The athlete showed team spirit.” “The laboratory report gave confirmation of the result.” Do not assume that every religious community uses the same ritual or gives a word the same specialised meaning.

practice.question: Choose the correct term: (a) belief in one God; (b) belief in many gods; (c) a person who does not believe that any god exists; (d) a person who regards the existence of gods as unknown or possibly unknowable.
practice.answer: (a) monotheism/monotheist; (b) polytheism/polytheist; (c) atheist; (d) agnostic.

practice.question: Match each word to its meaning: (a) principle; (b) doctrine; (c) dogma; (d) worship; (e) ritual.
practice.answer: (a) basic guiding rule or value; (b) set of teachings or beliefs; (c) authoritative teaching treated as unquestionable; (d) act of reverence or devotion; (e) established series of actions.

practice.question: Complete each sentence with one word: (a) The formal renunciation of a faith is called _____. (b) Washing as a religious preparation may be called _____. (c) Putting a person or object completely under water is _____. (d) A ceremony in some Christian traditions is called _____.
practice.answer: (a) apostasy; (b) ablution; (c) immersion; (d) confirmation.

practice.question: Write one neutral sentence using each of these words accurately: spirit, doctrine, worship, confirmation.
practice.answer: Accept four grammatical, contextually accurate sentences. Do not require a particular religious belief.
