lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Photography vocabulary: camera, lens, shutter and exposure
objectives: Define camera, lens, shutter, shutter release and film.
Explain shutter speed and its effect on recording movement.
Distinguish exposure, aperture, focus and shutter speed.
Use photography vocabulary accurately in context.
lessons.body:
Photography is the process of making images by recording light, usually with a camera. A camera is the device that controls and records the image. The lens is the optical part that gathers and focuses light onto the camera's sensor or film. Focus describes how sharply the subject appears; an image that is out of focus looks blurred.
The shutter is the mechanism that controls how long light reaches the sensor or film. Shutter speed is the length of time the shutter remains open. A fast shutter speed can help freeze a moving subject; a slower speed can record movement as blur and may require the camera to be held steadily. The shutter release is the button or control used to take the photograph and activate the shutter.
Film is a light-sensitive material used in traditional cameras to record images. Many modern cameras use an electronic sensor instead of film. Exposure is the amount of light recorded by the sensor or film. Exposure depends mainly on aperture, shutter speed and sensitivity (often described as ISO). Aperture is the adjustable opening in the lens through which light passes. These settings work together: changing one may require changing another to produce a suitable exposure.
A simple process is to choose the subject, compose the frame, focus the lens, select suitable exposure settings and press the shutter release. A photographer should consider available light, movement and the distance to the subject. The words camera, lens, shutter, shutter release, film and shutter speed name different parts or stages of the process; they are not interchangeable.

practice.question: Match each photography word to its function: (a) camera; (b) lens; (c) shutter; (d) shutter release; (e) film; (f) shutter speed.
practice.answer: (a) device that records an image; (b) optical part that gathers/focuses light; (c) mechanism controlling light entry time; (d) control used to take the photograph; (e) light-sensitive recording material; (f) length of time shutter remains open.

practice.question: Complete each sentence: (a) The part that gathers and focuses light is the _____. (b) The button used to take the photograph is the _____. (c) A fast _____ can help freeze movement. (d) Traditional cameras may record images on _____. (e) The amount of light recorded is called _____.
practice.answer: (a) lens; (b) shutter release; (c) shutter speed; (d) film; (e) exposure.

practice.question: Explain the difference between a shutter and shutter speed.
practice.answer: The shutter is the mechanism that opens and closes to control light; shutter speed is the duration for which it remains open.

practice.question: State two factors a photographer should consider before taking a photograph.
practice.answer: Any two: available light, subject movement, distance to subject, focus, composition or suitable exposure settings.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adverb formation, kinds and functions in sentences
objectives: Explain how adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs and whole clauses.
Form common adverbs from adjectives, including spelling changes and exceptions.
Recognise adverbs of manner, place, time, frequency and degree, and sentence and linking adverbs.
Use adverbs naturally in complete sentences and distinguish commonly confused forms.
lessons.body:
An adverb is a word or phrase that adds information to a verb, an adjective, another adverb or sometimes a whole clause. In “The team worked carefully”, carefully tells how they worked. In “The water is extremely cold”, extremely modifies the adjective cold. In “She spoke very quietly”, very modifies the adverb quietly. In “Fortunately, the rain stopped”, fortunately comments on the whole statement.

Many adverbs of manner are formed from adjectives by adding -ly: quick → quickly; bad → badly; cautious → cautiously. If an adjective ends in consonant + y, change y to i before adding -ly: happy → happily; easy → easily. Some adjectives ending in -le lose the final e before -ly: gentle → gently; simple → simply. An adjective ending in -ic commonly takes -ally: basic → basically; automatic → automatically. Learn irregular spellings individually: true → truly; whole → wholly. Not every adverb ends in -ly, and not every word ending in -ly is an adverb.

Some words have the same adjective and adverb form: a fast runner / run fast; a hard task / work hard; an early train / arrive early. Do not confuse hard (with effort) with hardly (almost not), or good (adjective) with well (usual adverb): “She is a good singer”; “She sings well”. Late means after the expected time; lately means recently. Choose by meaning and sentence function, not by appearance alone.

Adverbs have different functions. Adverbs of manner tell how (carefully, loudly); place tells where (outside, nearby); time tells when or for how long (yesterday, soon); frequency tells how often (often, rarely); and degree tells how much or to what extent (very, almost, quite). Sentence adverbs express a speaker's attitude (fortunately, perhaps), while linking adverbs connect ideas (however, therefore). A linking adverb is not a coordinating conjunction: write “It rained; however, we continued” or “It rained. However, we continued.”

An adverb can appear in different positions. Frequency adverbs usually come before a main verb (“They often practise”) but after the verb be (“They are often early”). Manner adverbs commonly follow the verb or its object (“The pupil answered politely”; “She packed the books carefully”). Time and place adverbs often appear at the end (“We met outside yesterday”). Position can change emphasis, so make sure the sentence remains clear.

practice.question: Form the adverbs from these adjectives: happy, gentle, basic, true, cautious. Give the spelling rule for any two.
practice.answer: happily, gently, basically, truly, cautiously. For example, consonant + y changes y to i before -ly (happy → happily); -le loses final e before -ly (gentle → gently).

practice.question: Identify the kind or function of each adverb in context: (a) The choir sang beautifully. (b) We will leave tomorrow. (c) Musa rarely misses class. (d) The bag is extremely heavy. (e) Fortunately, nobody was hurt.
practice.answer: (a) manner; (b) time; (c) frequency; (d) degree; (e) sentence adverb expressing the speaker's attitude.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct identification

practice.question: Choose the correct word in each sentence: (a) She plays the piano (good/well). (b) The workers tried (hard/hardly). (c) We arrived (late/lately) for the meeting. (d) The athlete ran (fast/fastly).
practice.answer: (a) well; (b) hard; (c) late; (d) fast.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct choice

practice.question: Rewrite each sentence using the adverb in brackets in a natural position: (a) The pupils complete their work. (carefully) (b) I visit my grandmother. (often) (c) The visitors waited. (outside)
practice.answer: (a) The pupils complete their work carefully. (b) I often visit my grandmother. (c) The visitors waited outside.

marking.criterion: One mark for each sentence with a natural, grammatical adverb position

practice.question: Write three original sentences: one with an adverb of manner, one with an adverb of frequency and one with a sentence adverb. Underline each adverb and name its function.
practice.answer: Possible answers: “The nurse spoke gently” (manner); “We usually read after school” (frequency); “Perhaps the team will win” (sentence adverb). Other grammatical original examples earn credit.

marking.criterion: Three grammatical original sentences, one mark each
Correctly underlines the adverb in each sentence

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The simple present: tense, time and use
objectives: Distinguish grammatical tense from the time an event refers to.
Explain the simple present for habits, general truths and occupations or stable situations.
Form affirmative, negative and interrogative simple-present sentences with correct subject–verb agreement.
Match simple-present examples to their intended meanings.
lessons.body:
Tense is a grammatical feature of a verb that helps locate an event or state in time. Time is the real-world idea of when something happens (past, present or future); tense is the verb form or construction used to express that time. The two ideas are related but are not identical. For example, the simple present can describe a future timetable: “The bus leaves at six tomorrow.” English commonly uses present and past verb forms; future time is often expressed with words and constructions such as will, be going to and present forms used in context.

The simple present is used for habits and repeated actions: “He works long hours”; “I practise the piano every evening.” It is also used for general truths and facts: “The world is round”; “Water boils at about 100°C at sea level.” It can describe a person's occupation or a relatively stable situation: “She sells bread”; “My uncle teaches science.” The time expression and meaning help you choose the use; the simple present does not normally mean that an action is happening at this very moment.

With most subjects, use the base form of the verb: I work; you work; they work. With he, she, it or a singular noun, add -s or -es: he works, she watches, the bus passes. If a verb ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: study → studies. Vowel + y keeps the y: play → plays. Have becomes has with he, she and it. Be has the forms am, is and are. Do becomes does in the third-person singular. In negatives and questions, use do or does with the base verb: “She does not walk to work”; “Does she walk to work?” Do not add another -s to the main verb after does.

Match each example to its meaning. “He works long hours” describes a regular pattern or occupation. “She walks to work” describes a repeated routine. “The world is round” states a general truth. Compare “She walks to work” with “She is walking to work now”: the first is a habit; the second is an activity in progress. For an action happening around the present moment, the present continuous is usually more suitable.

Use the simple present carefully in complete sentences. A singular subject takes a singular verb form (“The pupil reads”); a plural subject takes the base form (“The pupils read”). Adverbs of frequency such as usually, often and rarely commonly appear before the main verb (“She often reads”) but after be (“She is often punctual”).

practice.question: Explain the difference between tense and time in your own words. Give one example in which a present-tense form refers to future time.
practice.answer: Time is when an event happens; tense is the grammatical verb form or construction used to locate it. Example: The bus leaves at six tomorrow.

marking.criterion: Accurately distinguishes time from grammatical tense
Gives a grammatical present-form timetable example with future reference

practice.question: State whether each sentence expresses a habit/repeated action, a general truth, or an occupation/stable situation: (a) The earth moves around the sun. (b) Amina visits her aunt on Sundays. (c) My father repairs bicycles.
practice.answer: (a) general truth; (b) habit/repeated action; (c) occupation.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct classification

practice.question: Complete each sentence with the correct simple-present form: (a) She ___ (watch) the news. (b) The pupils ___ (study) English. (c) He ___ (have) a new dictionary. (d) ___ your brother ___ (walk) to school?
practice.answer: (a) watches; (b) study; (c) has; (d) Does your brother walk to school?

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct form or question construction

practice.question: Correct the errors: (a) She do not sells bread. (b) The bus leave at seven tomorrow. (c) They goes to class every day.
practice.answer: (a) She does not sell bread. (b) The bus leaves at seven tomorrow. (c) They go to class every day.

marking.criterion: Corrects auxiliary and base verb in (a)

practice.question: Write one original sentence for each use of the simple present: a repeated habit, a general truth and an occupation or stable situation. Underline the main verb in each.
practice.answer: Possible answers: I read before bed (habit); Plants need water (general truth); My aunt drives a bus (occupation). Other grammatical examples earn credit.

marking.criterion: Correctly underlines the main verb in each

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adjective-to-adverb conversion: forms and exceptions
objectives: Convert common adjectives to appropriate adverb forms.
Recognise irregular or unchanged forms including well, hard and truly.
Use converted forms accurately in context and distinguish hard from hardly.
lessons.body:
An adverb is often formed from an adjective, but the form is not always made by adding -ly. Use the meaning and grammar of the sentence to choose the correct form.

For the nine words in the source exercise, the appropriate forms are: quick → quickly; bright → brightly; careful → carefully; bad → badly; good → well; deep → deeply; clearer → more clearly; hard → hard; true → truly. “Clearer” is already a comparative adjective, so the natural comparative adverb is more clearly. Deep can also be used as an adverb in some contexts (“dig deep”), while deeply is common for figurative or emotional meanings (“deeply moved”). Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not. Good is an adjective; well is its usual adverb counterpart, although well can also be an adjective meaning healthy. True changes to truly, not truely.

Check each answer in a complete sentence. “The bright lamp shines brightly”; “She explained the rule clearly”; “He worked hard”; “I could hardly hear the announcement.” A correct word form can still be wrong if it does not fit the intended meaning. Read the whole sentence before deciding.

practice.question: Give the adverb forms of all nine words: quick, bright, careful, bad, good, deep, clearer, hard and true.
practice.answer: quickly, brightly, carefully, badly, well, deeply (also deep in suitable contexts), more clearly, hard, truly.

marking.criterion: One mark for each appropriate adverb form; accept deep where a natural adverbial use is intended

practice.question: Choose the correct form: (a) The students listened (careful/carefully). (b) The athlete trained (hard/hardly). (c) The message was (clearer/more clearly) explained the second time. (d) The patient is recovering (good/well).
practice.answer: (a) carefully; (b) hard; (c) more clearly; (d) well.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct choice

practice.question: Explain the difference between hard and hardly, and use each correctly in an original sentence.
practice.answer: Hard means with effort or intensity; hardly means almost not. Example: “They worked hard”; “I could hardly see the sign.”

marking.criterion: Two grammatical sentences using the forms correctly

practice.question: Correct the error in each sentence: (a) She sings good. (b) He truely answered. (c) The team played fastly.
practice.answer: (a) She sings well. (b) He truly answered. (c) The team played fast.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct correction

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Gradable and complementary antonyms: original practice
objectives: Explain the distinction between gradable and complementary antonyms.
Supply valid original word-pair examples for each type.
Classify antonyms using degrees, middle values and clearly defined contexts.
lessons.body:
Antonyms are words with contrasting meanings. Two useful groups are gradable antonyms and complementary antonyms. The spelling of the second term is complementary, not “complimentarity”.

Gradable antonyms are opposite ends or contrasting points on a scale. Examples include hot/cold, tall/short, wide/narrow and easy/difficult. There can be degrees between the two ends: water may be warm rather than hot or cold, and a person may be of medium height. We can use modifiers such as very, fairly, rather and slightly: very hot, slightly cold. In a question, “How hot is it?” allows a range of answers.

Complementary antonyms describe alternatives that normally exclude each other within the same clearly defined context. Examples include present/absent, open/closed and true/false. If a learner is recorded as present or absent for one lesson, the register normally assigns one of those two statuses. There is no ordinary middle degree such as “slightly present”. Define the context carefully: a door may be partly open, so open/closed can admit a boundary case in everyday use; the pair is treated as complementary when the task requires a single fully open or fully closed status.

To test a pair, ask: can something be between the two terms, or can one term be true to a greater or lesser degree? If yes, the pair is usually gradable. Can the same item, at the same time and under the same definition, be neither one nor the other? If the categories exhaust the possibilities, the pair is complementary. Do not classify a pair from the words alone when the context changes its meaning.

practice.question: Explain the difference between gradable and complementary antonyms. Give two original pairs for each group.
practice.answer: Gradable antonyms are contrasting points on a scale with possible degrees between them, e.g. hot/cold and wide/narrow. Complementary antonyms are mutually exclusive alternatives within a defined context, e.g. present/absent and true/false.

practice.question: Classify each pair as usually gradable or complementary, and give a reason: (a) rich/poor; (b) asleep/awake; (c) wide/narrow; (d) pass/fail on a test with a fixed pass mark.
practice.answer: (a) gradable: degrees of wealth exist; (b) complementary in the ordinary contrast: a person is asleep or awake at a given moment, though transitions can occur; (c) gradable: widths vary by degree; (d) complementary within the stated test rule: the result is either pass or fail.

marking.criterion: A sound contextual reason for each classification

practice.question: A learner says that warm proves hot/cold are not antonyms. Explain why this is incorrect. Then explain why context matters when classifying open/closed.
practice.answer: Warm is a middle degree on the same temperature scale, which is exactly why hot/cold are gradable antonyms. Open/closed may be treated as complementary when a rule requires fully open or fully closed, but a door can be partly open in ordinary use; the context and definition matter.

marking.criterion: Explains the scale and middle degree for hot/cold
Explains the contextual boundary for open/closed

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Descriptive and narrative essays: plans, models and writing
objectives: Plan a descriptive essay around a dominant impression and relevant sensory details.
Develop a descriptive paragraph with logical spatial or thematic organisation.
Plan a narrative with setting, participants, problem, turning point and outcome.
Write coherent descriptive and narrative responses using consistent tense and viewpoint.
lessons.body:
A descriptive essay helps a reader form a clear picture of a person, place, object or experience. Choose one dominant impression before writing: for example, a lively market, a peaceful school garden or a frightening storm. Select details that support that impression. Use sight, sound, smell, touch and, where relevant, taste; do not list every sensation mechanically. Arrange details in a clear order, such as from the entrance to the far end of a place, from near to far, or from the general view to important details.

Worked descriptive plan — “A busy market morning”:
- Opening: identify the market, time and dominant impression (energetic and crowded).
- Arrival: movement at the entrance; traders arranging goods; early sounds.
- Main scene: colours and arrangement of fruit, vegetables and fabrics; calls of sellers; footsteps and bargaining.
- Close detail: the smell of fresh produce and spices; a careful description of one stall.
- Ending: show the market becoming busier and restate the impression without repeating the opening.

Model descriptive paragraph: “By seven o’clock, the market was already awake. Baskets of tomatoes formed bright red islands beside heaps of green peppers, while folded fabrics hung in neat, colourful rows. Sellers called their prices across the narrow lanes. A handcart rattled over the uneven ground, and the smell of ripe bananas mixed with the sharp scent of fresh ginger. At one stall, a woman arranged oranges into a careful pyramid, replacing each fruit that rolled out of place. Everywhere, people moved with purpose, yet each small space seemed to have its own rhythm.” The details support the dominant impression of an active market.

A narrative essay tells a connected story. It normally has a setting, characters or participants, a situation, a problem or change, a turning point and an outcome. Arrange events in a sequence the reader can follow. Use a consistent point of view (I/we for first person; he/she/they for third person), past tense for a past story, and time links such as at first, later, meanwhile and eventually. Dialogue can reveal character or move the action, but use it selectively and punctuate it clearly.

Worked narrative plan — “The day I helped a stranger”:
- Setting and opening: a rainy afternoon on the way home; narrator notices an older passenger struggling with bags.
- Development: a bus arrives; the crowd moves quickly; one bag falls and its contents scatter.
- Problem: traffic and rain make it difficult to gather the items; the passenger is worried about missing an appointment.
- Turning point: narrator asks nearby people to help and retrieves the papers before they blow away.
- Outcome and reflection: the passenger catches the bus, thanks the helpers; narrator reflects on practical kindness.

Model narrative paragraph: “The rain began just as I reached the bus stop. People crowded beneath the small shelter, watching the road. An elderly man stood near the kerb with two heavy bags. When a bus pulled in, one bag slipped from his hand and oranges rolled across the wet pavement. Without thinking, I stepped forward. A woman beside me helped gather the fruit while another passenger held the bus door open. We returned the bags to the man, who smiled with relief and climbed aboard. As the bus moved away, I realised that a few minutes of attention had made a difficult journey easier for someone else.”

Before drafting, turn the title into a focused plan. After drafting, check that every paragraph serves the topic, events or details are logically ordered, verb tenses and viewpoint are consistent, and punctuation is accurate. A strong ending should complete the description or story rather than introduce an unrelated idea.

practice.question: Prepare a descriptive plan for “A quiet evening in my neighbourhood”. State the dominant impression and list at least five relevant details in a logical order.
practice.answer: A suitable plan identifies a peaceful/settled evening as the dominant impression and sequences details such as fading light, quieter traffic, neighbours returning home, cooking smells, birds settling, streetlights and distant conversation. Other coherent plans earn credit.

marking.criterion: At least five relevant sensory or observational details

practice.question: Write an original descriptive paragraph of about 100–130 words based on your plan in Q1.
practice.answer: Responses will vary. A successful paragraph maintains the stated impression, selects relevant concrete details, uses sensory language naturally, follows a clear order and is grammatically controlled.

marking.criterion: Unity and relevance to the title

practice.question: Plan a short narrative for “An unexpected act of kindness”. Include setting, participants, problem, turning point and outcome.
practice.answer: Responses will vary. A suitable plan establishes where/when the story happens, identifies the people involved, presents a believable difficulty, shows a clear action that changes events, and ends with a logical result or reflection.

practice.question: Write an original narrative of about 120–150 words using your plan in Q3.
practice.answer: Responses will vary. A successful narrative has connected events, consistent viewpoint and tense, a clear turning point, appropriate time links and a complete ending.

marking.criterion: Development of characters/setting and turning point
Consistent viewpoint, tense and linking expressions

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Original replacement assignment: adverbs and the simple present
objectives: Apply Week 7 adverb forms and functions in original sentences.
Apply the simple present for habits and general truths.
Use subject–verb agreement and do/does correctly in questions and negatives.
Complete a keyed, marked original assignment replacing unavailable prescribed questions.
lessons.body:
Original replacement assignment for an unavailable prescribed exercise. The original textbook page, exercise questions, edition and answer key were not supplied, so this activity is newly written and is not presented as a transcription or reconstruction of that exercise. It consolidates the Week 7 English topics evidenced in the scheme and source: adverbs and the simple present.

Complete all ten questions. Read each sentence carefully and use grammar and meaning together. Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or whole clauses. They express manner, place, time, frequency or degree, among other functions. The simple present commonly expresses habits, general truths and occupations or stable situations. Check subject–verb agreement: he/she/it usually takes -s or -es in affirmative clauses; negatives and questions use does plus the base verb.

The questions below are original. Each is worth two marks, for a total of twenty marks. The key gives an acceptable answer; other grammatical answers may be accepted where the question allows original examples.

practice.question: Identify the adverb and name its function: “The learners listened attentively.”
practice.answer: attentively — adverb of manner.

practice.question: Change the adjective careful into an adverb and use it in a complete sentence.
practice.answer: carefully; e.g. The nurse carefully checked the list.

practice.question: Choose the correct word: “The mechanic worked (hard/hardly) to repair the bus.” Explain briefly.
practice.answer: hard; it means with effort, whereas hardly means almost not.

practice.question: Place often correctly: “Musa is late for class.”
practice.answer: Musa is often late for class.

practice.question: Write one original sentence containing an adverb of degree.
practice.answer: Example: The water is very cold. Other grammatical examples such as “She was almost ready” are acceptable.

marking.criterion: Uses an adverb of degree correctly in a complete sentence

practice.question: Complete: “My sister ___ (teach) mathematics at the centre.”
practice.answer: teaches.

practice.question: State whether this simple-present sentence expresses a habit or a general truth: “The earth moves around the sun.”
practice.answer: A general truth.

practice.question: Make a question using does and the verb visit: “your uncle / the library”.
practice.answer: Does your uncle visit the library?

marking.criterion: Uses base verb visit and correct question order

practice.question: Correct the sentence: “She do not walks to school.”
practice.answer: She does not walk to school.

practice.question: Write one original simple-present sentence about a regular activity and add a suitable adverb of frequency.
practice.answer: Example: I usually revise my notes after dinner. Other grammatical examples are acceptable.

marking.criterion: Suitable adverb of frequency in a natural position

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Entertainment vocabulary and contextual reading: original replacement assignment
objectives: Explain key vocabulary associated with theatre, athletics and organised entertainment.
Use entertainment vocabulary accurately in context and original sentences.
Read an original passage for stated facts, vocabulary in context, inference and main idea.
Answer a keyed comprehension assessment and apply the vocabulary in writing.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL REPLACEMENT ACTIVITY — ENTERTAINMENT VOCABULARY AND READING

This activity is newly written to provide practice aligned with the Week 3 entertainment vocabulary topic. It is not a transcription of Effective English for SS 1 page 148, Countdown in English page 169, or Countdown page 352 Passage A. Those published pages and their questions were not supplied, and this activity does not claim to reproduce them.

Entertainment includes activities and events that people watch, listen to or take part in for enjoyment. In a theatre, an actor performs a role, the cast is the group of performers, the director guides the production, an usher assists the audience, and the box office handles ticket sales. A curtain call takes place when performers return to the stage after the performance to receive applause. In sport, a referee enforces the rules of a match; an assistant referee may help judge whether the ball has crossed a boundary. In athletics, a marathon is a long-distance race, a podium is a raised platform for award recipients, and a tracksuit is clothing worn for exercise or warm-up. A contingent is a group representing a school, club or country at an event.

READING PASSAGE: THE SCHOOL CULTURE EVENING

The students of Hillview Senior School had planned a culture evening to raise money for the school library. The event was to include a short play, a poetry recital, traditional music and a friendly five-a-side football match. The organising committee appointed Ada as director of the play because she had experience guiding performances. Twelve students formed the cast. They rehearsed after lessons, while two ushers volunteered to guide visitors to their seats.

On the evening, the box office opened at five o'clock. The tickets were inexpensive, and many parents arrived early. The first performance began promptly. The actors spoke clearly, and the audience listened attentively. At the end, the performers returned to the stage for a curtain call. Their families applauded enthusiastically.

Outside, the football match attracted another crowd. A referee explained the rules before the teams began. When the ball crossed the touchline, an assistant referee raised a flag. The players accepted the decision and continued. No one was injured, and both teams congratulated each other after the final whistle.

The evening ended with a short presentation. The principal thanked the organising committee, performers, officials and visitors. The school had not only raised money for new library books; it had also given students an opportunity to develop confidence, cooperation and organisational skills. The committee agreed to make the culture evening an annual event.

Read the passage and answer the questions. Select the best answer for each multiple-choice item. Questions 1–18 are worth one mark each.

practice.question: What was the main purpose of the culture evening?
options: To raise money for the school library
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Which activities were included in the programme?
options: A debate and a swimming race only
A play, poetry, traditional music and football
A marathon and a film screening
A spelling contest and a lecture
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Why was Ada appointed director?
practice.answer: C

practice.question: In the passage, the word 'cast' means:
practice.answer: A

practice.question: What did the ushers volunteer to do?
practice.answer: C

practice.question: At what time did the box office open?
practice.answer: B

practice.question: The phrase 'began promptly' suggests that the performance:
practice.answer: A

practice.question: What happened during the curtain call?
options: The performers returned to the stage
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Which word in the passage means people who come to watch an event?
practice.answer: C

practice.question: Who enforced the rules of the football match?
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Why did the assistant referee raise a flag?
practice.answer: C

practice.question: The players' response to the decision shows that they were:
practice.answer: A

practice.question: Which of the following is the best meaning of 'enthusiastically' as used in the passage?
practice.answer: B

practice.question: What two benefits did the principal's remarks identify?
options: Confidence and cooperation, as well as organisational skills
Better examination grades and free uniforms
practice.answer: B

practice.question: What can be inferred about the organising committee?
options: It planned the event and worked with others to deliver it
It had no interest in the library
practice.answer: A

practice.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Football should replace theatre at school
A well-organised school event can entertain people and build useful skills
Parents should organise every school activity
Only professional performers can entertain an audience
practice.answer: B

practice.question: In theatre, the 'box office' is mainly responsible for:
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Which title best suits the passage?
practice.answer: B

practice.question: Give suitable meanings for these entertainment words: marathon, podium, contingent, tracksuit, usher and curtain call.
practice.answer: Marathon: a long-distance running race; podium: a raised platform for award recipients; contingent: a group representing an organisation or country; tracksuit: clothing worn for exercise or warm-up; usher: a person who guides or assists an audience; curtain call: performers' return to the stage after a performance to receive applause.

marking.criterion: One mark for each accurate meaning

practice.question: Use any four of these words in original, grammatically correct sentences: actor, cast, director, referee, box office, penalty.
practice.answer: Responses vary. Each sentence must use the selected word accurately in context.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct sentence and accurate word use

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 6 affixes: extended prefixes and suffixes
objectives: Explain and exemplify the remaining Week 6 prefixes.
Form and interpret adjectives ending in -less.
Distinguish derivational -en and -ize/-ise from grammatical tense endings.
Apply plural -es and -ies patterns in context.
Correctly answer and mark the source's four-suffix evaluation using accurate terminology.
lessons.body:
A prefix is added before a base word; a suffix is added after it. An affix changes or adds to the meaning or grammatical form of the base. Always check that the resulting word is established and that it fits the sentence.

Additional prefixes in this unit:
- extra- means outside or beyond: extracurricular (activities outside the formal curriculum).
- ex- can mean former, or out/from in words of Latin origin: ex-president (a former president), export (send goods out).
- inter- means between or among: international (between nations).
- trans- means across or from one state/place to another: transport (carry from one place to another).
- post- means after: post-war (after a war).
- pre- means before: pre-school (before formal schooling).
- super- means above, over or exceptionally: superhuman (beyond ordinary human ability).
- sub- means under or below: submarine (a vessel that operates under water).
- ab- can mean away or from in words such as abduct (take away by force) and abnormal (away from the normal).
- un- commonly gives a negative or opposite meaning: unfair, unknown, untie. The source prints “unn-”; this is not the standard prefix spelling. Treat it as a likely source typographical error, not a separate affix.
- ante- means before: antenatal (before birth).
- anti- means against: anti-war (opposed to war). Ante- and anti- are not interchangeable.
- arch- can mean chief or principal, and in some words conveys extreme: archbishop (a senior bishop), arch-enemy (chief enemy).

The suffix -less means without or lacking: childless (without children), odourless (without a noticeable smell), penniless (without money), heartless (without compassion), useless (not useful). The ending changes the meaning of the base; it commonly forms adjectives. It does not mean that the base is simply absent in every possible sense, so interpret the whole word in context.

The source labels a group “tense suffixes” and includes -en and “-ze”. These are not tense endings in the same way as -ed. They are word-forming suffixes that commonly make verbs. The suffix -en can mean make or become: strengthen (make stronger), deafen (make deaf or cause hearing loss), brighten (make brighter), widen (make wider). Smoothen is used by some speakers, but smooth is also a verb and is often the simpler choice. The source examples strengthen, deafen, brighten, smoothen and widen are not all equally common in every variety.

The source's “-ze” examples practicalize and mobilize point to the verb-forming suffix commonly written -ize in some spelling systems. British English dictionaries also commonly use -ise for many of these words; mobilise and mobilize are accepted spelling variants. “Practicalize” is uncommon and may sound awkward; in most contexts, put into practice or make practical is clearer. Do not treat -ze by itself as a tense marker. The suffix helps form a verb from a noun or adjective.

Plural -es is a grammatical ending, not the same kind of word-building suffix as -less or -ize. Add -es to many nouns ending in s, x, z, ch or sh: buses, boxes, quizzes, churches, dishes. Consonant + y usually changes to -ies: baby/babies, fly/flies. This plural objective is also taught in the existing noun lesson; the practice below checks the distinction.

When analysing a word, identify the base, identify the affix, explain the change in meaning or word class, and use the result in a sentence. Check unusual forms in a reliable dictionary rather than assuming every prefix or suffix can attach to every base.

practice.question: Give the meaning of each prefix and one correct example: extra-, inter-, trans-, post-, pre-, super-, sub-, ante-, anti- and arch-.
practice.answer: extra- outside/beyond (extracurricular); inter- between (international); trans- across (transport); post- after (post-war); pre- before (pre-school); super- above/beyond (superhuman); sub- under (submarine); ante- before (antenatal); anti- against (anti-war); arch- chief/principal (archbishop).

marking.criterion: One mark for each accurate meaning-example pair

practice.question: The source prints “unn-”. Write the standard prefix form and use it in two words. Explain the difference between ante- and anti- with one example of each.
practice.answer: The standard form is un-: unfair, unknown, untie. Ante- means before (antenatal); anti- means against (anti-war).

marking.criterion: Correct un- spelling and two examples
Accurate distinction and examples for ante-/anti-

practice.question: Explain the meaning of -less and form suitable words from child, odour, penny and heart. Use any two in sentences.
practice.answer: childless, odourless, penniless, heartless. Sentences must use the words accurately, e.g. The room was odourless; the heartless action upset the class.

practice.question: Form verbs using -en from strong, bright, deaf and wide. Explain what the suffix contributes.
practice.answer: strengthen, brighten, deafen, widen. -en forms verbs meaning make or become the quality expressed by the base.

practice.question: The source labels -en and “-ze” as tense suffixes. Explain why this label is misleading, and give two examples of each word-forming suffix.
practice.answer: -en and -ize/-ise form verbs from bases; they do not mark tense in the way -ed does. Examples: strengthen, widen; mobilize/mobilise, modernize/modernise. The source's practicalize is uncommon; put into practice is often clearer.

marking.criterion: Distinguishes word formation from tense marking

practice.question: Complete the plurals: church, box, dish, baby, fly and quiz.
practice.answer: churches, boxes, dishes, babies, flies, quizzes.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct plural

practice.question: Write two examples each of words formed with -less, -ize/-ise, -es and -en. Label which endings form adjectives, verbs or plurals.
practice.answer: Examples: harmless, childless (-less adjectives); mobilize/mobilise, modernize/modernise (-ize/-ise verbs); boxes, churches (-es plurals); strengthen, widen (-en verbs).

marking.criterion: Two accurate examples for each ending
Correctly identifies adjective, verb and plural functions

practice.question: Correct the statements: (a) anti- means before; (b) -less forms past tense; (c) mobilize is a past-tense form; (d) “unn-” is the standard spelling of the negative prefix.
practice.answer: (a) ante- means before; anti- means against. (b) -less forms adjectives meaning without/lacking. (c) mobilize is a verb formed with -ize, not a past tense. (d) un- is the standard prefix spelling.

marking.criterion: One mark for each accurate correction

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 6: two-syllable word stress
objectives: Identify first-syllable stress in the Week 6 source list.
Recognise common prefix-related words with second-syllable stress without applying a false universal rule.
Compare noun/verb stress and identify pairs that do not shift.
Mark stress in an original parallel evaluation and consult pronunciation dictionaries.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — Week 6 word stress

Word stress is the syllable that receives the strongest prominence. Dictionaries mark primary stress with /ˈ/ immediately before the stressed syllable. In class, capitals can show the same pattern: BA-sic means the first syllable is stressed. Do not force a three-syllable word into a two-syllable rule.

FIRST-SYLLABLE LIST
The source list is retained as a study list. In a British English reference model, first-syllable stress is heard in BA-sic, SOL-emn, CRED-it, COL-lar, CHRIS-tian, CER-tain, FOR-tune, HAT-red, HAM-let, CAP-tain, VIC-tor, STU-pid and MAN-sion. PERIOD is also printed in the source list, but it has three syllables (PE-ri-od), not two; its first syllable is stressed. This is a source classification issue, not a reason to alter the source text.

PREFIX-RELATED SECOND-SYLLABLE EXAMPLES
Some common two-syllable words have a weak first element and stronger second syllable: a-BOVE, a-BOUT, a-GAIN, be-FORE, be-HIND, be-LOW, be-SIDE, be-COME, re-TURN and re-LAX. This is a pattern to notice, not a universal rule that every word beginning with a prefix must stress its second syllable. A prefix can be stressed in other words; check the actual word in a pronunciation dictionary.

NOUN/VERB PAIRS
Some two-syllable pairs change stress with word class: CON-tent (noun: material or information) / con-TENT (verb: satisfy); IM-port (noun: goods brought into a country) / im-PORT (verb: bring goods into a country). Other pairs do not show the same shift: con-SENT (noun and verb) and re-FORM (noun and verb, in the common British pronunciation for improvement/to improve). Identify the sense and check a dictionary; do not assume every noun/verb pair changes stress.

SOURCE EVALUATION NOTE
The source prints “constract” and “baggar” in its seven-word stress exercise. These spellings are not silently corrected or assigned invented pronunciations here. This supplement supplies a clearly labelled original parallel assessment using unambiguous words. A teacher may later confirm the intended source spellings from the original page.

PRACTICE METHOD
Divide the word into syllables; look up the headword; find /ˈ/; listen to the agreed accent model; say the word naturally; then use it in a sentence. Written identification and oral production are different outcomes. The examples and exercises below are original teaching materials; no dictionary passage or exercise is reproduced.

practice.question: Mark the stressed syllable in: basic, solemn, credit, collar, Christian, certain, fortune, period, hatred, Hamlet, captain, victor, stupid and mansion. (14 marks)
practice.answer: BA-sic; SOL-emn; CRED-it; COL-lar; CHRIS-tian; CER-tain; FOR-tune; PE-ri-od; HAT-red; HAM-let; CAP-tain; VIC-tor; STU-pid; MAN-sion. Period has three syllables.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correctly marked word; accept PE-ri-od as three syllables.

practice.question: Mark the main stress in these ten original second-syllable examples: above, about, again, before, behind, below, beside, become, return and relax. (10 marks)
practice.answer: a-BOVE; a-BOUT; a-GAIN; be-FORE; be-HIND; be-LOW; be-SIDE; be-COME; re-TURN; re-LAX.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correctly identified second-syllable stress.

practice.question: For each pair, state whether noun and verb stress changes: content, import, consent and reform. Mark both forms and explain one pair. (8 marks)
practice.answer: CONTENT noun CON-tent / verb con-TENT; IMPORT noun IM-port / verb im-PORT; CONSENT noun and verb con-SENT; REFORM noun and verb re-FORM. Stress changes in content and import, not in consent and reform in the reference pronunciations used here.

marking.criterion: Consent pair correctly marked as unchanged
Reform pair correctly marked as unchanged
Explains that word class does not guarantee a stress shift

practice.question: ORIGINAL PARALLEL EVALUATION. Mark the main stress in: hotel, relax, arrive, begin, message, market and mistake. (7 marks)
practice.answer: ho-TEL; re-LAX; ar-RIVE; be-GIN; MES-sage; MAR-ket; mis-TAKE.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correctly marked word.

practice.question: Explain why “all two-syllable words with prefixes stress the second syllable” is unsafe. Identify one source-list issue. (4 marks)
practice.answer: Stress depends on the individual word; some prefixed words stress the first syllable, so check a dictionary. Period has three syllables, not two. “Constract” and “baggar” are not safely corrected by guessing.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 6 story writing: “It is a man’s world”
objectives: Plan a coherent story with opening, complication, rising action, climax and resolution.
Use consistent past tense and viewpoint.
Explore the assigned topic through believable characters and events.
Write an original story assessed with a transparent 25-mark rubric.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — Week 6 story writing: “It is a man’s world”

A story presents connected events involving characters in a setting. It needs an opening, a complication, rising action, a climax and a resolution. Keep the events coherent. For this task, use the simple past tense for the main events and maintain one viewpoint unless a deliberate change is needed.

UNDERSTANDING THE TOPIC
“It is a man’s world” is an expression about places or systems where men have traditionally held more power or opportunity. A writer may explore the expression critically: show an assumption or barrier, how a character responds, and what the experience reveals. Avoid claiming that every man behaves alike or that all women share one experience. Let believable events develop the theme rather than turning the story into a lecture.

WORKED PLAN — “The Workshop Door”
Setting: A town technical training centre preparing for a community skills exhibition.
Main character: Tola, an apprentice who has practised repairing small electrical devices.
Other characters: Mr Ade, the workshop supervisor; Kunle, another apprentice; exhibition visitors.
Opening: The display generator fails on the morning of the exhibition. Tola offers to help diagnose it.
Complication: A visitor assumes that only male apprentices should handle the equipment. Kunle hesitates, while Tola is asked to prepare the registration desk.
Rising action: Tola asks the supervisor to let her carry out the checks. She isolates the power, follows safety procedures, studies the wiring diagram and finds a loose connector. Kunle assists by holding an inspection lamp.
Climax: The generator fails again during the final test. Tola notices that the fuel line is kinked. Mr Ade confirms the problem; the team corrects it safely.
Resolution: The generator runs steadily. Tola explains the fault-finding process to visitors. The centre introduces a fair skills rota so every apprentice can practise each task.
Reflection: Skill should be judged by preparation, care and performance, not assumptions about gender.

MODEL STORY — “The Workshop Door”
The first time Tola entered the technical workshop, she noticed the smell of machine oil and the neat rows of tools on the wall. She had joined the centre because she enjoyed finding out how things worked. For weeks, she had practised checking plugs, replacing damaged leads and reading simple wiring diagrams under her instructor's supervision.

On the morning of the community skills exhibition, the small generator beside the display stand refused to start. Mr Ade, the workshop supervisor, asked the apprentices to help find the fault. Tola stepped forward, but a visitor glanced at her and said, “Surely one of the boys should handle the machine.”

Kunle looked uncomfortable. Tola felt her face grow warm, but she did not argue. She asked Mr Ade whether she could carry out the first checks while he supervised. He agreed. She switched off the unit, isolated the power and followed the workshop's safety procedure. Then she compared the connections with the wiring diagram. One connector was loose.

“Good observation,” Mr Ade said. “Let's secure it and test the unit safely.”

Kunle held the inspection lamp while Tola checked the connection. The generator started, but it stopped again during the next test. Tola did not rush. She retraced the steps, checked the fuel line and noticed that it had been bent against the frame. Mr Ade confirmed the problem. Together they repositioned the line and completed the safety checks before restarting the generator.

This time it ran steadily. When the visitors arrived, Mr Ade invited Tola to explain how the team had traced the fault. She described each step and showed them the diagram. The visitor who had doubted her ability listened carefully and later thanked her for the explanation.

After the exhibition, the centre introduced a rota so that every apprentice could practise inspection, repair and testing under supervision. Tola was pleased that the change would help others learn too. She had not needed to prove that women were better than men; she had shown that ability grows through learning, practice and fair opportunity. The workshop door, she thought, should be open to anyone willing to learn and work safely.

WRITING TASK
Write your own original story on “It is a man’s world”. Plan the events, build to a climax and keep the main narrative in the simple past tense. You may interpret the expression critically or describe a character's experience. Create your own characters, setting, problem and ending; do not copy the model.

25-MARK RUBRIC
| Criterion | What the marker looks for | Marks |
|---|---|---:|
| Relevance and theme | Meaningfully explores the assigned topic | 3 |
| Plot and sequence | Events are coherent and logically ordered | 4 |
| Development and climax | A complication develops and reaches a convincing high point | 4 |
| Characters and setting | People and place are clear and believable | 3 |
| Tense and viewpoint | Main events use a consistent past tense and viewpoint | 3 |
| Description and dialogue | Details and dialogue support the action | 2 |
| Paragraphing and cohesion | Paragraphs and time links guide the reader | 2 |
| Grammar, spelling and punctuation | Language is accurate and clear | 4 |
| TOTAL |  | 25 |

Mark only what the learner writes. Do not award theme marks merely because the title is repeated. A reasoned critical interpretation is acceptable; learners need not agree with the expression.

practice.question: Arrange these stages in a workable order: resolution; complication; setting and characters; climax; opening situation; rising action. (6 marks)
practice.answer: Setting and characters; opening situation; complication; rising action; climax; resolution.

marking.criterion: One mark for each stage in a workable order.

practice.question: Identify two actions that create the complication and two that lead to the resolution in the model. (4 marks)
practice.answer: Complication: the visitor assumes a boy should handle the machine; Tola is redirected to the registration desk. Resolution: Tola identifies the loose connector and later the kinked fuel line under supervision; the team tests the generator and introduces a fair skills rota.

practice.question: Write an original story on “It is a man’s world”. Plan the events, build to a climax and keep the main narrative in the simple past tense. Apply the 25-mark rubric. (25 marks)
practice.answer: Responses vary. Assess the learner's own story against the eight rubric criteria; do not require the model plot or a particular opinion.

marking.criterion: Apply the complete 25-mark rubric criterion by criterion.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 6 original reading equivalents: comprehension, syllables and stress
objectives: Complete original comprehension and summary activities as equivalents for unavailable prescribed reading pages.
Divide words into syllables and identify primary stress using dictionary conventions.
Apply reading-for-detail, inference and summary skills to original passages.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT READING TASKS — Week 6

The scheme points learners to three textbook assignments that are not present in the supplied source archive. The tasks below are original, curriculum-aligned equivalents. They do not reproduce, reconstruct or claim to have inspected Complete English Course pages 420–423, Standard Speech 10 Book page 23, or Countdown WASSCE/SSCE English Language pages 5–7. Each task can be completed from the material printed here.

TASK A — READING FOR DETAIL, INFERENCE AND SUMMARY (equivalent for the missing Complete English Course reading)
Passage: “The Repair Café”
A youth centre opened a monthly repair café to help residents extend the life of household items. Volunteers first inspected each item and explained whether it could be repaired safely. A team repaired a desk lamp by replacing a damaged plug, while another group tightened the loose handle of a cooking pot. The volunteers refused to work on a cracked electrical casing because it required a qualified technician. Visitors were encouraged to ask questions and learn how to care for their belongings. At the end of the day, the centre recorded twelve successful repairs and referred three unsafe items to specialist services. The organiser said the aim was not to repair everything, but to reduce waste while putting safety first.
Answer in complete sentences:
1. What was the purpose of the repair café?
2. Name two items that volunteers repaired.
3. Why did they refuse to work on the cracked electrical casing?
4. What can you infer about the centre's attitude to safety?
5. Write a two-sentence summary using only the passage's main points.

TASK B — SYLLABLES AND WORD STRESS (equivalent for the missing Standard Speech 10 Book diction page)
A syllable is a beat or unit of pronunciation organised around a vowel sound. A word may have one or several syllables. A pronunciation dictionary uses a dot or syllable break to show division and /ˈ/ immediately before the main stressed syllable. Stress is a feature of spoken pronunciation; spelling alone does not reliably show it.
Study these original examples: TA-ble (two syllables, first stressed); a-BOVE (two syllables, second stressed); BA-na-na (three syllables, second stressed); COM-pu-ter (three syllables, second stressed); re-LAX (two syllables, second stressed).
1. Divide remember, market, education and begin into syllables.
2. Mark the main stress in TA-ble, a-BOVE, BA-na-na, COM-pu-ter and re-LAX.
3. Explain the difference between a syllable and a stressed syllable.
4. Look up one of the words in a pronunciation dictionary and state what the stress mark tells the reader.
Written identification does not prove oral production. Listening and speaking require a model and later observation.

TASK C — READING COMPREHENSION AND SUMMARY (equivalent for the missing Countdown pages)
Passage: “A Community Reading Room”
A group of residents converted an unused room beside the market into a small reading room. They collected donated books, repaired the shelves and arranged the books by subject. A retired teacher volunteered twice a week to help younger readers choose suitable books. The group kept a simple register so that borrowed books could be returned. During the first month, thirty-two people visited the room, including traders who came before opening their stalls. The organisers plan to add newspapers and large-print books when more donations arrive.
1. Where is the reading room?
2. Name two preparations the residents made.
3. How often does the retired teacher volunteer?
4. Why is a register useful?
5. What can be inferred about the reading room's likely benefit to traders?
6. Write a two-sentence summary.

MARKING GUIDE — 30 MARKS
Task A (10): purpose 1; two repaired items 2; safety reason 2; supported inference 2; concise accurate summary 3.
Task B (10): accurate syllable divisions 4; five stress marks 2; syllable/stress distinction 2; dictionary stress-mark explanation 2. Accept recognised accent variants where the dictionary records them.
Task C (10): location 1; two preparations 2; twice a week 1; register purpose 2; supported inference 1; concise accurate summary 3.
Award marks for evidence, not for copying the passage at length.

practice.question: Complete Task A — The Repair Café. Answer all five passage questions and write the two-sentence summary. (10 marks)
practice.answer: Purpose: help residents extend the life of household items safely. Repaired items: desk lamp and cooking-pot handle. The cracked electrical casing was unsafe and required a qualified technician. Inference: the centre puts safety before the number of repairs. Summary should state that volunteers repaired suitable items, referred unsafe ones and aimed to reduce waste safely.

practice.question: Complete Task B — Syllables and Word Stress. Divide the four words, mark the five examples and answer the two explanation questions. (10 marks)
practice.answer: remember: re-mem-ber; market: mar-ket; education: ed-u-ca-tion; begin: be-gin. Stress examples: TA-ble; a-BOVE; ba-NA-na; com-PU-ter; re-LAX. A syllable is a pronunciation unit; a stressed syllable is the one given greatest prominence. /ˈ/ comes immediately before the main stressed syllable.

practice.question: Complete Task C — A Community Reading Room. Answer all six questions and write the two-sentence summary. (10 marks)
practice.answer: The room is beside the market. Residents collected donated books, repaired shelves and arranged books by subject. The retired teacher volunteers twice a week. The register records borrowing so books can be returned. Traders may visit before opening their stalls. Summary should state that residents created a reading room from an unused room, organised donated books and attracted local readers.

lessons.title: Week 6 original weekend revision: vocabulary, synonyms and determiners
objectives: Apply vocabulary knowledge in multiple-choice questions.
Choose nearest-in-meaning words in context.
Select accurate articles and determiners in complete sentences.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL PARALLEL WEEKEND REVISION — Week 6

The source weekend assignment contains five vocabulary multiple-choice questions, five nearest-in-meaning questions and five article/determiner choices, but it has no reliable answer key or mark allocation and several items are garbled. This original parallel set assesses the same broad skills without guessing or silently repairing the source items. Each item carries one mark. Total: 15 marks.

SECTION A — VOCABULARY (5 marks)
Choose the best answer.
1. A person who repairs electrical wiring is an: (a) electrician (b) editor (c) architect.
2. A place where books are kept for reading or borrowing is a: (a) laboratory (b) library (c) factory.
3. If a task is postponed, it is: (a) delayed (b) completed (c) repeated.
4. A person who gives help without payment is a: (a) volunteer (b) passenger (c) spectator.
5. To preserve something is to: (a) protect it from damage (b) throw it away (c) hide it permanently.

SECTION B — NEAREST IN MEANING (5 marks)
Choose the nearest meaning of the bold word.
6. The teacher asked us to **assist** the new pupil. (a) help (b) disturb (c) ignore.
7. The instructions were **brief**. (a) short (b) confusing (c) loud.
8. The room was **vacant**. (a) empty (b) noisy (c) crowded.
9. She gave a **generous** donation. (a) large and willing (b) unwilling (c) careless.
10. The class must **observe** the safety rules. (a) follow (b) forget (c) invent.

SECTION C — ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS (5 marks)
Choose the correct option.
11. We saw ___ eagle above the field. (a) a (b) an (c) the.
12. Please return ___ book you borrowed from me. (a) a (b) an (c) the.
13. There is ___ water left in the bottle; it is enough for one person. (a) a few (b) a little (c) many.
14. ___ pupils who completed the task may leave. (a) This (b) Those (c) Much.
15. She has ___ useful dictionary on her desk. (a) a (b) an (c) the.

KEY AND MARKING
1 a; 2 b; 3 a; 4 a; 5 a; 6 a; 7 a; 8 a; 9 a; 10 a; 11 b; 12 c; 13 b; 14 b; 15 a. Award one mark for each correct answer. Total 15 marks.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct response.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct response.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct response.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 4 original equivalents: drama, phrases, agriculture and reading
objectives: Study an original short drama extract, identify dramatic features and answer keyed comprehension questions.
Apply noun-phrase and verb-phrase knowledge in original practice.
Read an original agriculture passage and answer detail, inference and vocabulary questions.
Practise spelling in context using a reviewed original list.
Complete an original 12-item reading-comprehension assessment as an equivalent for the unavailable Passage B.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT ACTIVITIES — 1st Term Week 4

The scheme refers to five textbook assignments whose pages, editions and answer keys are not in the supplied source archive. The activities below are newly written, curriculum-aligned equivalents. They do not reproduce or claim to have inspected Effective English pages 68–71, Countdown page 236, Countdown pages 144–145, Countdown Passage B pages 353–354, or Count down in English by Evans pages 58–62.

ACTIVITY 1 — ORIGINAL DRAMA EXTRACT AND COMPREHENSION
Title: The Exhibition Table
Characters: Nneka, a student preparing a science display; Musa, her classmate; Mrs Danjuma, the teacher.
Scene: A classroom after lessons. A large table stands near the window. Nneka enters carrying a box of labelled models.
NNEKA: Musa, the display table is still covered with old exercise books. The exhibition begins tomorrow.
MUSA: I moved them yesterday, but another class put them back. We should ask before moving anyone's things.
NNEKA: I have asked twice. I am worried that our models will be left on the floor.
(Musa checks the noticeboard and points to a timetable.)
MUSA: The timetable says our class has the room from four o'clock. It is only half past three. Let's take the boxes to the cupboard and ask Mrs Danjuma to help us arrange the table.
(Mrs Danjuma enters.)
MRS DANJUMA: What is the difficulty?
NNEKA: We need a safe place for the models and enough time to arrange the display.
MRS DANJUMA: You were right to check the timetable. Put the fragile models on the lower shelf, keep the walkway clear and write a short note to the other class. I will speak to their teacher.
MUSA: Then we can arrange the table when our time begins.
NNEKA: Thank you. We can finish without disturbing anyone.
(Musa carries the box carefully to the cupboard. Nneka writes the note. Mrs Danjuma checks that the walkway is clear.)
Curtain.

Questions:
1. Where and when does the scene take place?
2. What problem does Nneka face?
3. Why does Musa check the noticeboard?
4. What does Mrs Danjuma advise them to do?
5. Give one example of a stage direction.
6. Identify the main conflict in the scene.
7. What can you infer about Musa's attitude to other classes?
8. How is the problem resolved?
9. Suggest another suitable title.
10. Summarise the scene in two sentences.

ACTIVITY 2 — FURTHER DRAMA STUDY (equivalent for the unavailable drama pages)
A play is written to be performed. Dialogue is what characters say; stage directions indicate actions, movement, tone or setting; a scene is a unit of action in a particular time or place; a character is a person represented in the play; conflict is a problem or opposing desire that drives the action. Props are objects used by performers. The audience watches and interprets both speech and action.
Task: Identify two characters, the setting, one prop, one stage direction and the conflict in “The Exhibition Table”. Explain one way the stage directions help an actor or audience understand the scene.

ACTIVITY 3 — NOUN PHRASE AND VERB PHRASE PRACTICE (equivalent for Countdown page 236)
A noun phrase is built around a noun or pronoun head: “the three careful learners”. A verb phrase contains a main verb and may include auxiliary verbs: “have been preparing”.
For each sentence, identify the noun phrase named in brackets and underline the complete verb phrase:
1. The new science club meets on Friday. (subject noun phrase)
2. Our teacher has arranged the display. (verb phrase)
3. The visitors admired the colourful models. (object noun phrase)
4. The class will have completed the work by noon. (verb phrase)
5. To read widely improves vocabulary. (infinitive phrase functioning as subject)
6. Swimming before breakfast refreshes him. (gerund phrase functioning as subject)

ACTIVITY 4 — AGRICULTURE READING AND VOCABULARY (equivalent for Countdown pages 144–145)
Passage: “Protecting the School Farm”
The agriculture club noticed that heavy rain was washing loose soil from the school farm. The members planted grass along the edges of the beds and used dry leaves as mulch. Their teacher explained that plant roots hold soil together and that mulch reduces the direct impact of rain. The club also made shallow channels to guide excess water away without cutting deep trenches. After several weeks, the beds retained more soil and the vegetables grew well. The learners recorded the changes in a notebook so that they could compare the results later.
Questions:
1. What problem did the club notice?
2. Name two methods used to protect the soil.
3. What does mulch do?
4. Why did the learners keep a notebook?
5. Explain “excess” as used in the passage.
6. Give a suitable title other than the one supplied.

ACTIVITY 5 — SPELLING AND VOCABULARY IN CONTEXT (equivalent for Count down in English pages 58–62)
Choose the correctly spelt word:
1. accomodation / accommodation
2. neccessary / necessary
3. seperate / separate
4. recieve / receive
5. maintenence / maintenance
6. equipement / equipment
7. enviroment / environment
8. aggriculture / agriculture
9. oportunity / opportunity
10. commitee / committee
Then use any three correctly in original sentences.

ACTIVITY 6 — ORIGINAL WEEKEND PASSAGE B (equivalent for Countdown Passage B, questions 19–30)
Passage: “A Shared Workshop”
A community centre opened a shared workshop where residents could borrow simple tools for supervised repairs. Before borrowing an item, each person signed a register and checked that the tool was safe to use. Volunteers demonstrated how to handle hammers, screwdrivers and measuring tapes. The centre did not lend electrical tools to beginners without supervision. At the end of each week, a volunteer inspected the returned tools, cleaned them and reported any damage. The project helped residents complete small repairs and taught them to use equipment responsibly.
Choose the best answer:
19. What did the centre open? (a) a clinic (b) a shared workshop (c) a market (d) a library.
20. What did a borrower sign? (a) a register (b) a receipt for food (c) a timetable (d) a letter.
21. Which tool is named in the passage? (a) telescope (b) screwdriver (c) compass (d) microscope.
22. Why were electrical tools restricted? (a) they were too heavy (b) beginners needed supervision (c) they were decorative (d) they were not returned.
23. Who inspected returned tools? (a) every borrower (b) a volunteer (c) a shopkeeper (d) a visitor.
24. What happened to tools after inspection? (a) they were sold (b) they were cleaned (c) they were hidden (d) they were discarded.
25. The word “supervised” most nearly means: (a) watched and guided (b) forgotten (c) repaired secretly (d) borrowed permanently.
26. “Responsible” in the passage means: (a) careless (b) dependable and careful (c) noisy (d) unwilling.
27. What can be inferred about the register? (a) It helps track borrowed tools. (b) It repairs the tools. (c) It teaches spelling. (d) It replaces supervision.
28. Which statement is true? (a) All electrical tools were lent freely. (b) Volunteers demonstrated safe handling. (c) No tools were inspected. (d) Borrowers never signed anything.
29. What is the main purpose of the project? (a) to sell tools (b) to support small repairs and responsible use (c) to replace schools (d) to train professional builders only.
30. Which title best fits the passage? (a) A Shared Workshop (b) A School Competition (c) A Lost Register (d) The Market Road.

ANSWER AND MARKING GUIDE — 53 MARKS
Activity 1 (10): 1 classroom after lessons; 2 table occupied/models at risk; 3 to confirm the room timetable; 4 store fragile models safely, clear walkway and write a note; 5 any accurate parenthetical direction; 6 access to the display table without disturbing another class; 7 considerate/respectful; 8 teacher intervention and scheduled access; 9 any suitable title; 10 accurate two-sentence summary. One mark each.
Activity 2 (6): two characters 2; setting 1; prop 1; stage direction 1; conflict/helpful explanation 1.
Activity 3 (6): one mark for each correct phrase/function or verb phrase.
Activity 4 (6): one mark each for correct detail, function or contextual meaning.
Activity 5 (13): one mark for each of ten spellings; one mark for each of three accurate original sentences.
Activity 6 (12): 19 b; 20 a; 21 b; 22 b; 23 b; 24 b; 25 a; 26 b; 27 a; 28 b; 29 b; 30 a. One mark each.
Total: 53 marks. Activity 5 carries 13 marks, so the overall total is 53, not 52.

practice.question: Answer Activity 1 — The Exhibition Table. (10 marks)
practice.answer: 1. A classroom after lessons. 2. The table is occupied and the models may be left on the floor. 3. To confirm when the class may use the room. 4. Store fragile models safely, keep the walkway clear and write a note. 5. Any parenthetical action, e.g. “Musa checks the noticeboard”. 6. The class needs the table without disturbing another class. 7. He is considerate and wants to respect others' property. 8. The teacher confirms the timetable and helps arrange safe access. 9. Any suitable title. 10. Two accurate sentences summarising the problem and resolution.

marking.criterion: One mark for each accurate answer.

practice.question: Complete Activity 2 — Further Drama Study. (6 marks)
practice.answer: Characters: Nneka, Musa, Mrs Danjuma. Setting: classroom after lessons. Prop: box of models/noticeboard/table. Stage direction: any parenthetical direction. Conflict: access to a display table and safe storage. Stage directions guide actors' actions and help the audience picture events.

marking.criterion: Conflict or explanation of stage direction

practice.question: Complete Activity 3 — Noun Phrase and Verb Phrase Practice. (6 marks)
practice.answer: 1. The new science club — noun phrase subject. 2. has arranged — verb phrase. 3. the colourful models — noun phrase object. 4. will have completed — verb phrase. 5. To read widely — infinitive phrase as subject. 6. Swimming before breakfast — gerund phrase as subject.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct identification.

practice.question: Answer Activity 4 — Protecting the School Farm. (6 marks)
practice.answer: 1. Heavy rain was washing soil away. 2. Planting grass and using dry leaves as mulch; shallow channels are also acceptable. 3. Mulch reduces the direct impact of rain. 4. To compare results later. 5. More than needed / surplus. 6. Any suitable title.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct answer.

practice.question: Complete Activity 5 — Spelling and Vocabulary in Context. Choose all ten correct spellings and write three original sentences. (13 marks)
practice.answer: 1 accommodation; 2 necessary; 3 separate; 4 receive; 5 maintenance; 6 equipment; 7 environment; 8 agriculture; 9 opportunity; 10 committee. Sentences must use the selected words correctly.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct spelling
One mark for each accurate original sentence

practice.question: Complete Activity 6 — Original Weekend Passage B, questions 19–30. (12 marks)

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct option.

lessons.title: Week 8 original reading equivalents: comprehension, adjectives and argument
objectives: Read an original passage for stated details, supported inference and summary.
Identify adjectives, adjective phrases and adjectival clauses in context.
Analyse a short argument by identifying its claim, reasons, counterargument and response.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT READING ACTIVITIES — 1st Term Week 8

The scheme refers to three textbook reading assignments whose pages and editions are not included in the source archive. The activities below are original, curriculum-aligned equivalents. They do not reproduce or claim to have inspected Effective English Unit 3 page 54, Countdown in English page 209, or Countdown page 28.

ACTIVITY 1 — COMPREHENSION AND SUMMARY (equivalent for Effective English Unit 3, page 54)
Passage: “The School Garden Project”
A group of learners asked their head teacher for permission to turn an unused corner of the school grounds into a garden. They first cleared litter and marked out small beds. The agriculture teacher showed them how to loosen the soil and mix in compost. Each group planted a different vegetable and kept a record of watering and growth. When heavy rain threatened to wash the soil away, the learners added mulch and planted grass along the edges. At the end of the term, they harvested some vegetables for the school kitchen and used the rest to prepare seeds for the next planting season.
Questions:
1. What did the learners ask permission to do?
2. Name two preparations they made before planting.
3. What did the teacher show them?
4. How did they protect the soil from heavy rain?
5. What did they do with the harvest?
6. Write a two-sentence summary using only the main points.

ACTIVITY 2 — ADJECTIVES IN CONTEXT (equivalent for Countdown in English, page 209)
Read: “The busy market opened before sunrise. A narrow path between the stalls led to a clean, well-lit reading corner. The woman who managed the corner arranged books in labelled boxes. Several young visitors, eager to learn, sat beside the wooden table.”
Tasks:
1. Identify four adjectives that describe nouns.
2. Identify the adjective phrase in “eager to learn”.
3. Identify the relative clause in “who managed the corner”.
4. Explain the difference between an adjective, an adjective phrase and an adjectival clause.
5. Write one original sentence containing an adjective phrase and one containing an adjectival clause.

ACTIVITY 3 — READING AN ARGUMENT (equivalent for Countdown, page 28)
Passage: “Why Every School Needs a Reading Club”
A reading club gives learners a regular time to read beyond their class assignments. Members can recommend books, discuss ideas and practise explaining what they have understood. Some people argue that clubs take time away from sports and other activities. However, a club can meet once a week and can be organised around learners' interests. A well-run reading club does not replace classroom teaching; it gives learners another opportunity to build vocabulary, confidence and curiosity.
Questions:
1. State the writer's main claim.
2. Give two reasons supporting the claim.
3. Identify the counterargument.
4. What is the writer's response to the counterargument?
5. Write a one-sentence conclusion that supports the claim without repeating it word for word.

MARKING GUIDE — 20 MARKS
Activity 1 (8): permission 1; two preparations 2; teacher's guidance 1; soil protection 1; use of harvest 1; accurate two-sentence summary 2.
Activity 2 (7): four adjectives 2; adjective phrase 1; relative clause 1; accurate distinction 1; two original sentences 2.
Activity 3 (5): main claim 1; two supporting reasons 2; counterargument 1; response/conclusion 1.
The missing textbook pages are not represented as source material, and no answer is inferred from them.

practice.question: Complete Activity 1 — The School Garden Project. (8 marks)
practice.answer: 1. To turn an unused corner into a garden. 2. Cleared litter and marked beds. 3. How to loosen soil and mix compost. 4. Added mulch and planted grass along the edges. 5. Some vegetables went to the school kitchen; others provided seeds. 6. Two accurate sentences describing the garden project, soil care and harvest.

practice.question: Complete Activity 2 — Adjectives in Context. (7 marks)
practice.answer: Adjectives include busy, narrow, clean, well-lit, young, wooden. Adjective phrase: eager to learn. Relative/adjectival clause: who managed the corner. An adjective is a word class; an adjective phrase is a phrase functioning as a modifier; an adjectival clause is a clause that modifies a noun. Original sentences must include each required structure.

practice.question: Complete Activity 3 — Reading an Argument. (5 marks)
practice.answer: Claim: every school needs a reading club. Reasons: regular reading beyond class assignments; discussion/recommendations build understanding, vocabulary and confidence. Counterargument: clubs take time from sports and other activities. Response: weekly meetings can fit around learners' interests. Conclusion should support the claim in original words.
